docs.title: Welcome to Chromaticity
docs.text: Chromaticity is a real-time audio-reactive VJ performance and shader authoring engine built for live shows, club booths, and livestreams.

docs.title: Getting Started in 60 Seconds
docs.text:
• Choose your audio input in Settings — Chromaticity hot-swaps audio inputs live without interrupting stage output.
  • Launch a scene from Library or press ⌘K / Ctrl+K to jump straight to any scene or tool.
  • Perform live with Scene Controls, Meta Controls, and 8 instant Snap slots (1–8).
  • Open your stage output with GO LIVE in the top bar, or toggle the STAGE monitor dock from any workspace.

docs.title: About Chromaticity
docs.text: Chromaticity is a cross-platform GPU shader performance instrument and visual mixer built in Rust, wgpu, Tauri, and Svelte 5.

docs.title: Core Architecture
docs.text:
• Real-time Audio Analysis: Low-latency FFT band extraction, RMS/peak metering, onset detection, and live zero-restart input hot-swap.
  • Native .chroma Scenes: GLSL 4.50 shaders with JSON control schemas, sandboxed QuickJS scripting, and live Author IDE compilation.
  • Performance & I/O: Dedicated Perform and Mix decks, multi-monitor Stage Output, live Twitch RTMPS streaming, MIDI learn and performance bindings, bidirectional UDP OSC routing, and fMP4 recording/replay infrastructure.

docs.title: Audio Reactivity
docs.text: Chromaticity is an audio-reactive runtime: every scene can sample tempo, energy, and per-band spectrum data from the live audio input and bind them as GLSL uniforms. This page describes how audio enters the engine, how the analysis pipeline produces uniform snapshots, and how the operator HUD widgets and the GLSL shader binding layer consume that data.

docs.title: Audio path overview
docs.text:
The audio pipeline runs across three thread boundaries, established by the runtime thread-and-process model:

  1. Audio input — Operating-system audio capture is owned by the audio analysis thread. A frame-source implementation pulls interleaved sample data, mixes multi-channel input down to mono, and produces a fixed-shape AudioFrame value type.
  2. Analysis — The same thread calls extract_uniform_snapshot on each frame. The function is pure: same input frame yields the same output snapshot. Its responsibilities are RMS, peak, an eight-band log-spaced FFT, and a single-frame autocorrelation BPM estimate.
  3. Hand-off — The producer-side runtime publishes the snapshot into a shared Arc<Mutex<AudioUniformSnapshot>> cell. The scheduler tick reads the cell, marshals it to GPU uniform inputs for the render path, and emits it to the UI over the engine-to-UI IPC bridge.

The audio crate intentionally does not depend on the render or IPC crates; consumers marshal the plain-data snapshot into whatever surface they own. This is what lets the analysis thread stay render-agnostic and lets the IPC bridge attach without any audio-side churn.

docs.title: What the snapshot carries
docs.text:
Each tick publishes the following fields:

Field Range Notes bpm [50, 220] Estimated tempo, clamped to the musical range; defaults to 120 on too-short frames rms [0, 1] Root-mean-square energy of the mono-mixed frame, clamped at 1 for out-of-range PCM input peak [0, 1] Peak absolute magnitude of the mono-mixed frame fft_bands[8] [0, 1] per band Eight log-spaced FFT magnitudes covering 20 Hz to 20 kHz

The snapshot is a #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq)] value type; consumers can copy it freely without coordination. The default shape is the all-zero baseline that consumers see during the no-audio-yet startup window.

docs.title: The eight-to-four band reduction
docs.text:
The slice-1 producer publishes eight log-spaced FFT bands. Several operator-facing widgets expose four named bands ("bass", "low-mid", "mid", "high") to keep the UX legible. The reduction combines adjacent bands pairwise:

  • bass = (fft[0] + fft[1]) / 2
  • low-mid = (fft[2] + fft[3]) / 2
  • mid = (fft[4] + fft[5]) / 2
  • high = (fft[6] + fft[7]) / 2

This four-band view drives the AudioReactivity widget's named tile strip and the BPM strip below it. Authors who want raw eight-band resolution read chroma_AudioFFT directly in their GLSL.

docs.title: How the operator HUD uses live audio
docs.text:
Three visualizer widgets in the operator HUD read live audio over the IPC bridge:

  • AudioReactivity — Four named band tiles plus a tempo strip derived from bpm. The widget falls back to a synthetic time-domain function during the no-snapshot startup window so the UI is never blank.
  • BpmRing — Circular tempo indicator phase-locked to bpm. The ring's animation cadence reads the current snapshot directly; the synthetic fallback uses a fixed 120 BPM.
  • BeatDots — Discrete beat-pulse indicator that lights up on each beat boundary derived from bpm. The synthetic fallback fires at the same fixed tempo.

All three widgets implement a "live snapshot present" gate: when the last received snapshot is fresh, visuals run from real data; when the snapshot is stale or absent, the synthetic fallback paints. This dual mode is what lets the widgets ship as wireframe-faithful chrome before the live engine wiring lands and continue to work after the audio input source is silent.

The 48-bar FFT visualizer inside AudioReactivity and the inline 64-bar Spectrum surface in the Audio Uniforms view both stay synthetic-driven in the V1 release; live-driven retrofits are post-MVP UX work.

docs.title: Worked example: a radial pulse shader
docs.text:
A minimal scene that pulses on the bass band:

uniform float chroma_AudioFFT[8];
uniform float chroma_AudioRMS;
uniform vec2  iResolution;

void main() {
    vec2 uv  = (gl_FragCoord.xy - 0.5 * iResolution) / iResolution.y;
    float r  = length(uv);

    // Bass = bands 0 and 1 averaged.
    float bass  = 0.5 * (chroma_AudioFFT[0] + chroma_AudioFFT[1]);

    // Pulse: an inverse-distance ring that thickens with bass energy
    // and brightens with overall RMS.
    float pulse = smoothstep(0.40 - 0.20 * bass, 0.42, r)
                * (1.0 - smoothstep(0.42, 0.44 + 0.10 * bass, r));

    gl_FragColor = vec4(vec3(pulse * (0.5 + chroma_AudioRMS)), 1.0);
}

The same scene becomes a tempo-locked breathing pulse by mixing in chroma_BPMSin against the radius (imported .synScene packages are translated to these names automatically). Authors can compose any of the audio uniforms; the binding adapter publishes them all in a stable per-pass order so per-pass uniform-buffer slot indices stay stable across reloads.

docs.title: Setting the audio threshold
docs.text:
The audio noise-floor gate is exposed as the chroma_Threshold uniform and is operator-controllable through the audio settings panel and the OSC routes:

  • Shift+T samples the current 200 ms rolling RMS of chroma_Level and sets the threshold to that value (also reachable as /audio/threshold/sample).
  • /audio/threshold {float} accepts an absolute threshold in [0, 1].

Audio hops with RMS below the threshold publish zeroed chroma_*Level and chroma_*Hits family uniforms. The threshold is the operator's primary tool for rejecting room noise, HVAC bleed, and crowd murmur in quiet sections of a show.

Authored from engine/audio/src/runtime.rs (producer thread shape), engine/audio/src/uniforms.rs (snapshot field semantics), engine/render/src/audio_adapter.rs (uniform binding contract), and the docs/adr/ADR-019-audio-uniform-ipc-bridge.md IPC contract combined with the docs/adr/ADR-006-thread-and-process-model.md thread-affinity invariants. Clean-room per docs/29-cleanroom-legal-policy-baseline.md.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
A pattern catalogue for scene authors. Three top-level sections:

  1. Control design — how to lay out a scene's author-facing knobs so Perform, Snap, presets, and playlists stay composable.
  2. GLSL pitfalls — common foot-guns when writing shaders against the chroma_* uniform surface.
  3. GLSL performance — cost considerations, when to reach for Lygia, and the honest picture of what the V1 preview adapter does and doesn't render.

Read top-down on the first pass; each subsection is a named pattern or pitfall and is independently citable. If you only have five minutes, the four most leverage-y items are Control surface composability, Coerce booleans through > 0.5 (§2.2), Branchless over divergent branches, and The canvas-2d preview is not your scene.

docs.title: 1 — Control design
docs.text: A scene's CONTROLS array is the public API your scene exposes to operators, snaps, presets, OSC, MIDI, and the in-app preview adapter all at once. The fields are documented in Scene Workflow; this section covers what to do with them.

docs.title: 1.1 Pick the smallest control surface that exposes intent
docs.text:
Every control you declare becomes:

  • a row in Perform's Scene Controls panel,
  • a slot in every preset captured against this scene,
  • a value persisted into every Snap,
  • a route under /chroma/control/<name> for OSC operators,
  • a learnable target for MIDI bindings.

That's five surfaces multiplied by the count. Five controls is fine. Twenty is operator-hostile. Thirty is unusable in Perform.

A useful sieve: if two controls always move together in your own testing, fold them into one. A tint colour with a per-channel tint_r / tint_g / tint_b triplet adjacent to it is one control, not four. A position xy plus a separate position_x and position_y is one xy control, not three.

docs.title: 1.2 Name controls for the operator, not the shader
docs.text:
The NAME field is what the operator reads at perform-time. Two rules that age well:

  • Pick a short verb-or-noun phrase, lower-case, snake-cased. bass_pulse, palette_hue, tunnel_speed. Avoid GLSL-internal spellings like u_pulse_amp_norm.
  • Use the DESCRIPTION field for the longer story. Perform surfaces NAME as the row label; the description shows up in tooltips and in the operator's Help panel. There is no character budget on DESCRIPTION; treat it like a one-sentence operator-facing comment.

The LABEL legacy field is preserved for ingest of reference scenes but does not need to be authored on new scenes; NAME carries.

docs.title: 1.3 Snap-friendliness and the control surface as a state vector
docs.text:
The Snap system captures the full vector of every control's current value at the moment you save the slot. Recalling a slot writes every captured value back. Presets behave the same way under Wave 2.4 PERF.C semantics: Cmd-click captures, click recalls. Playlists transition between presets across scene boundaries.

The implication: every author-facing control is part of the scene's state vector. Two anti-patterns follow:

  • Don't include "moment-of-author" controls that you don't want operators to capture into Snaps. A debug show_uv toggle, a one- shot randomize_seed bang, a developer-only wireframe flag: drop these before publishing or move them behind your authoring branch.
  • Don't bake operator-facing logic into uniforms the scene hot-reloads under. A control that takes effect only on scene reload is silently broken under Snap recall — the recalled value will not match the visible state. Make controls react every frame, not at boot.

docs.title: 1.4 Use UI_GROUP to keep Perform legible
docs.text:
Controls without a UI_GROUP land in the default panel and stack top-to-bottom in declaration order. For scenes with more than ~6 controls, declare an explicit UI_GROUP per cluster. Perform respects the groups as collapsible panels under Scene Controls; the Library scene-detail pane shows the group taxonomy too.

A workable convention:

  • appearance — colours, palettes, tint, alpha.
  • motion — speed, rotation, warp, drift.
  • audio — per-band gains, reactivity multipliers.
  • geometry — scale, position, count, density.
  • meta-output — the four canonical IS_META flags (mirror, invert, global tint, master gain).
  • meta-pipeline — anything else that affects the global pipeline rather than the scene's intrinsic look.

The strings are operator-facing prose; pick what reads cleanly in your scene's domain. Stay consistent across scenes if you ship a library.

docs.title: 1.5 The IS_META flag and the _Reactivity meta-gate
docs.text:
IS_META: true on a control signals "this is a global pipeline adjustment, not an intrinsic scene parameter." The fixture set in engine/scene/tests/fixtures/scenes/meta-controls.chroma enumerates the canonical four:

  • meta_mirror (toggle)
  • meta_invert (toggle)
  • meta_tint (color)
  • meta_gain (slider, [0, 2])

Beyond those four, a separate first-class meta-control — _Reactivity — multiplies every audio uniform globally before the shader reads it. It's part of the Advanced edition meta-gate per the catalog and is what gives operators a single knob to turn down audio response without rewriting every shader's mix factor.

Pattern. Author your shader against the raw audio uniforms; reach for an IS_META audio_gain slider local to your scene only if you need scene-specific trim distinct from the global _Reactivity knob. Otherwise leave the global meta-knob to do its job.

docs.title: 1.6 Range, default, and the "interesting zone"
docs.text:
Three patterns that pay for themselves:

  • Set MIN and MAX to the range you actually want the operator to explore. A slider [0, 1000] where every interesting value lives in [0, 10] wastes the operator's fine motor control.
  • Pick DEFAULT at the most-compelling-looking sample of the range, not the midpoint and not zero. The operator's first encounter with your scene is the default. If 0.0 is dead-silent black, that's a bad first impression.
  • Avoid exact-zero defaults on multiplicative axes. A gain or intensity slider that starts at 0.0 makes the scene look broken at load time. Start at 0.5 and let the operator dial down.

docs.title: 1.7 Curves: smooth variants, knobs vs sliders
docs.text:
The TYPE field accepts the base kind plus a smoothing variant after the first whitespace token (slider smooth, bang smooth, xy smooth). The base kind drives the schema; the variant drives the runtime smoothing behaviour. Specifically:

  • slider vs knob — the engine treats both as scalar inputs through the same pipeline. Pick knob when the visual affordance in Perform should be rotary (small parameter, fits the dense scene-controls grid), slider when linear travel reads more intuitive (gains, levels, anything 0-to-1).
  • slider smooth etc. — apply the smoothing variant to any control the operator will sweep aggressively. The smoothing removes step-jaggies when the value is bound to MIDI faders or swept via OSC at high update rate.
  • bang vs bang smooth — momentary triggers. Smoothing on bang decays the trigger toward zero with a configurable half-life. Without smoothing, the trigger fires for exactly one frame.

The PARAMS field on a control carries variant-specific smoothing payload (target half-life, smoothing window, etc.) when the variant uses one.

docs.title: 1.8 How the preview adapter consumes named controls
docs.text:
The Perform / Library / Author preview tiles render through the canvas-2d procedural adapter (SceneCanvas.svelte), not through a GPU GLSL pipeline. The preview is wireframe-faithful for procedural shapes but is not rasterising your scene's actual shader. The ADR-011 GPU pipeline lands in Phase-2+; until then, the preview adapter reads three named pre-multiplier control names verbatim:

  • speed (slider in [0, 1], nominal 0.5) pre-multiplies the renderer's time argument. 0.0 freezes the preview, 1.0 runs at 2x.
  • intensity (slider in [0, 1], nominal 0.5) pre-multiplies the renderer's audio-level argument with the same 2x scaling.
  • tint (vec3 or vec4 in [0, 1] per channel) draws a translucent overlay over the procedural vignette at 20% of the supplied alpha.

Plus four control-coverage extras: invert, mirror, hor_mirror / horizontal_mirror, vert_mirror / vertical_mirror. These render as post-pass overlays at the canvas-2d adapter level.

Pattern. If you want your scene's preview tile to "do the right thing" without operators having to imagine the GPU render, name your top-level speed / intensity / tint controls exactly those three spellings. The preview adapter will respect them. Other controls still dispatch through the runtime command bus to the engine — they're just not visualised in the canvas-2d preview.

docs.title: 2 — GLSL pitfalls
docs.text: This section catalogues mistakes that compile cleanly but produce silently-wrong visuals at runtime. Read Chromaticity Uniforms for the canonical uniform vocabulary before reaching here for debugging.

docs.title: 2.1 A typo at the uniform declaration site silently binds zero
docs.text:
The runtime does not perform per-binding casing fixups. If your shader declares uniform float chroma_audiorms; (lowercase r) instead of chroma_AudioRMS, the binding adapter has no symbol to publish into. The compile is clean. The uniform reads zero forever. The scene renders dark.

Pattern. Copy uniform names from the Chromaticity Uniforms reference verbatim. The scene loader surfaces a warning at load time when a declared uniform name fails to resolve against the catalog; check the load diagnostics on every fresh declaration. Don't rely on visual inspection — a uniform binding zero often looks like the scene "just needs more audio."

docs.title: 2.2 Coerce toggles through > 0.5, not == 1.0
docs.text:
GLSL toggles arrive as float uniforms (0.0 or 1.0 on disk). The trip from operator → IPC → JSON → uniform → shader passes through several float coercions; a value that started life as 1.0 may arrive as 0.9999937 by the time the shader reads it. Comparing for strict equality against 1.0 produces sporadic flickering when the toggle is "on but reads slightly less than perfect."

// FRAGILE — equality against a coerced float
if (u_invert == 1.0) {
    col = vec3(1.0) - col;
}

// ROBUST — half-range threshold
if (u_invert > 0.5) {
    col = vec3(1.0) - col;
}

The same rule applies to if (audio_band == 0.0) checks; use < 1e-6 or similar. CPU integer comparisons are not GPU float comparisons; thinking in epsilons is the discipline.

docs.title: 2.3 Integer-vs-float coercion at uniform boundaries
docs.text:
GLSL implicitly promotes integer literals in expressions, but the rules surprise people. A common pitfall:

// WRONG — integer division, returns 0
float t = 1 / 2;

// RIGHT — float division, returns 0.5
float t = 1.0 / 2.0;

This bites authors who copy patterns from CPU languages where literal integer division promotes. In GLSL, 1 / 2 is 0, full stop, and many downstream errors look like "the scene is dark" or "the colours desaturated."

Similarly, when sampling chroma_AudioFFT[i], declare i as int explicitly:

int idx = int(floor(t * 8.0));
idx = clamp(idx, 0, 7);
float band = chroma_AudioFFT[idx];

A float-indexed array access compiles on some GLSL versions and fails on others; the int cast is portable.

docs.title: 2.4 Out-of-bounds array sampling
docs.text:
chroma_AudioFFT[8] has exactly eight bands, indices 0..7. Reading chroma_AudioFFT[8] (the off-by-one) is undefined behaviour: some drivers return 0, some return the next memory cell, some kernel- panic the GPU on tiles where unused registers carry old fragment state. Always clamp(idx, 0, 7) before indexing.

Sampler textures (chroma_Spectrum, chroma_LevelTrail) have the same constraint: the sampler API clamps automatically at the GL level, but the u coordinate you feed needs to be in [0, 1] for documented behaviour. Wrapping mode is sampler-default GL_CLAMP_TO_EDGE unless you opt into something else.

docs.title: 2.5 The all-zero baseline is real
docs.text:
Every chroma_* audio uniform reads zero during the no-audio-yet startup window. The first audio tick arrives some tens of milliseconds after the scene loads. A shader that divides by chroma_AudioRMS without an epsilon guard produces inf / NaN / black-screen on the first frame.

// FRAGILE — division by zero on first frame
vec3 col = base / chroma_AudioRMS;

// ROBUST — saturating fallback
float rms = max(chroma_AudioRMS, 1e-3);
vec3 col = base / rms;

The same pattern applies to chroma_AudioPeak, chroma_Level, chroma_BPMConfidence, and any time-accelerator (chroma_BassTime etc.) that decays toward zero on silence.

docs.title: 2.6 Alpha pre-multiplication caveats
docs.text:
Chromaticity scenes write to a 32-bit RGBA target. The compositor expects non-pre-multiplied alpha by default — i.e. your gl_FragColor carries the colour you want at full opacity and the alpha channel carries the blend factor. Authors who copy a pattern that pre-multiplies (multiplying RGB by A inside the shader) will see their scene appear dim when alpha is below 1.0.

// NON-PREMULTIPLIED (default)
gl_FragColor = vec4(scene_rgb, scene_alpha);

// PRE-MULTIPLIED (rare; use only with a matching blend mode)
gl_FragColor = vec4(scene_rgb * scene_alpha, scene_alpha);

If you need pre-multiplied (compositing-over with HDR sources, post-FX that operates in linear-light), document it in the scene's DESCRIPTION field so the operator knows what they're consuming.

docs.title: 2.7 gl_FragCoord is in pixels, not normalised
docs.text:
A new author's first instinct is often:

// WRONG — gl_FragCoord goes 0..width / 0..height, not 0..1
vec2 uv = gl_FragCoord.xy;

You want one of:

// Normalised, anisotropic — uv ranges 0..1 in each axis
vec2 uv = gl_FragCoord.xy / iResolution.xy;

// Normalised, aspect-corrected — centre at (0,0), keep y in [-0.5, 0.5]
vec2 uv = (gl_FragCoord.xy - 0.5 * iResolution.xy) / iResolution.y;

The aspect-corrected form is what audio-reactivity.md's worked example uses; it is the canonical shape for scenes that draw centred radial geometry.

docs.title: 2.8 Hot-reload preserves chroma_time, not your accumulators
docs.text:
Live-reload (docs/37) preserves the operator's control values across the reload by re-applying the captured PreservedState. It does not preserve in-shader-state like a feedback accumulator in a multipass FLOAT target — that target gets cleared and your post-reload first frame reads zero.

Pattern. Don't write logic that depends on the previous frame's contents surviving a hot-reload. If your scene needs warm-up state, seed it from a stable noise function of chroma_time or chroma_AudioTime so the same pattern reproduces on every reload.

docs.title: 3 — GLSL performance
docs.text: A 60 Hz render budget gives you ~16.67 ms per frame for everything: geometry, multipass composition, post-FX, plus the scheduler tick that drains audio and IPC. On a mid-range integrated GPU, that budget is generous for most scenes and tight for the worst-case ones. This section catalogues where cost actually accumulates.

docs.title: 3.1 Texture sampling is the largest single per-fragment cost
docs.text:
A modern GPU's texture sampler is fast but not free. A shader that does eight texture() calls per fragment will spend most of its budget in the sampler. The canonical mitigations:

  • Sample once, reuse. If you need chroma_AudioFFT[3] twice in your shader, store the first read into a local float and reuse. The compiler may CSE for you on simple cases, but for sampler reads through chroma_Spectrum it almost certainly will not.
  • Prefer the array uniform over the sampler. Reading chroma_AudioFFT[i] is a uniform fetch, not a sampler read. Reading texture(chroma_Spectrum, u).r is a sampler read. Use the array when you only need the eight-band shape; use the sampler when you need the full 256-or-512-bin spectrum.
  • Avoid texture sampling inside loops with variable bounds. GPU drivers can hoist loop-invariant samples; they can't always hoist conditional ones.

docs.title: 3.2 Prefer branchless arithmetic over uniform branching
docs.text:
GPU fragments execute in lockstep across a warp / wavefront (typically 32 or 64 lanes). When an if branches differently across lanes, both sides of the branch execute and the results are masked — the "diverged" cost is the sum, not the average.

A branchless pattern is often cheaper:

// DIVERGENT (per-fragment branch on a control value)
vec3 col;
if (u_audio_gate > 0.5 && bass > 0.1) {
    col = pulse_color * bass;
} else {
    col = base_color;
}

// BRANCHLESS (mix on the predicate)
float gate = step(0.5, u_audio_gate) * step(0.1, bass);
vec3 col = mix(base_color, pulse_color * bass, gate);

mix / step / smoothstep are sampler-grade fast paths on nearly every GPU. Use them in preference to per-lane control flow whenever the predicate is cheap.

The exception: when the branch is genuinely uniform across the warp (e.g. a toggle uniform that's the same for every fragment), GLSL compilers can collapse it to a true branch. That case is free. The expensive case is per-fragment divergence.

docs.title: 3.3 iTime / chroma_time cost vs iFrame
docs.text:
Both are scalar uniforms — the per-frame read cost is the same. What matters is what you do with them:

  • chroma_time (float seconds) is wallclock-aligned. Use it for animation phase, oscillators, wave functions. It is monotonically increasing within a session.
  • iFrame (integer frame counter) is useful for stochastic patterns that need to sample a different pseudo-random value per frame. Modular arithmetic on iFrame is your friend for temporal dither, accumulation, or frame-blending tricks.

The performance impact comes from the shape of the math you build on them. A sin(chroma_time * 6.283 * freq) is one transcendental per fragment; if you need that pattern many times, compute it once into a local and reuse. A nested-trig phase function like sin(cos(sin(t * a) * b) * c) may look concise but executes three transcendentals per fragment.

docs.title: 3.4 Lygia helpers vs hand-rolled math
docs.text:
Chromaticity ships Lygia v1.1.4 vendored under third_party/lygia/ (per Shader Sourcing Research). Lygia is a utility library — noise, SDF, blend, palette, raymarch helpers — that composes against the chroma_* uniforms cleanly.

When to reach for Lygia:

  • Noise functions: lygia/generative/cnoise.glsl (classic Perlin), lygia/generative/snoise.glsl (Simplex), lygia/generative/fbm.glsl (fractional Brownian motion), lygia/generative/voronoi.glsl (cellular). The vendored implementations are reference-quality ports of canonical algorithms.
  • SDF primitives: lygia/sdf/ carries sphereSDF, boxSDF, etc. Hand-rolling these is a foot-gun.
  • Colour conversions: lygia/color/ carries the standard sRGB / linear / HSL / OKLAB / palette helpers.

When to skip Lygia and hand-roll:

  • One-shot math that's smaller than the include. A single smoothstep doesn't need a helper file.
  • Performance-critical inner loops where the call boundary cost (or per-call uniform setup, if the helper expects extra arguments) is comparable to the helper's body.
  • Anything where you need exact control over WGSL transpile semantics (Phase-2+ when the GPU pipeline lands).

License-trial caveat. Lygia ships under Prosperity-3.0.0 with a 30-day commercial trial. The trial does not bind Chromaticity's shipped product — the license election lands at the Phase-5 EV-LICENSE-AUDIT gate. Treat Lygia as a foreground tool during authoring; pre-stage the MIT-licensed alternative (webgl-noise + glslify + three.js post-FX subsets per the Shader Sourcing Research shortlist) if you ship a scene library you intend to redistribute.

docs.title: 3.5 Multipass composition costs scale with pass count
docs.text:
The scene schema's PASSES array declares N render passes that compose into the final frame. Each pass:

  • Pays a framebuffer-bind cost (~tens of microseconds on a modern GPU).
  • Pays a texture-allocation cost on first use (one-time per pass).
  • Reads the previous pass's output as a sampler2D texture.

Three passes is generally cheap. Eight is generous but manageable. Twenty is asking the operator's integrated-GPU laptop to drop frames.

Pattern. Combine passes where the math allows it. If pass 2 does a horizontal blur and pass 3 does a vertical blur, that's a classic separable filter and is a clean two-pass design — keep it two. But if pass 4 does a colour grade that could fold into the final composite of pass 5, fold it.

The FLOAT per-pass flag (preserved in pass extensions at slice-3a) marks a pass as needing 16- or 32-bit per-channel precision; that doubles or quadruples the framebuffer memory footprint compared to a default 8-bit-per-channel target. Use FLOAT only when you need HDR or feedback accumulation precision.

docs.title: 3.6 The canvas-2d preview adapter is not your final render
docs.text:
The preview tiles in Perform / Library / Author are rendered by src/lib/widgets/SceneCanvas.svelte against the 16 procedural renderers in scene-renderers.ts. This is an operator preview adapter, not a GPU rasterisation of your shader. Specifically:

  • It runs on the main UI thread via requestAnimationFrame and HTML CanvasRenderingContext2D.
  • It resolves a SceneKind from your scene's metadata (title, tags, category) and picks one of 16 procedural patterns to display.
  • It honours the three named pre-multipliers (speed, intensity, tint) plus the four mirror / invert post-pass flags described in §1.8 above.
  • It reads the live audio snapshot when present so the preview pulse responds to real audio.

What it does not do:

  • Execute your main.glsl source.
  • Render your multipass chain.
  • Resolve lygia/ includes.
  • Respect any uniform other than the named pre-multipliers above.

ADR-011 Phase-2+ work will replace the preview adapter with a real wgpu-backed mini renderer that does run your shader. Until then, the preview communicates "this is what the scene's about" rather than "this is what your shader literally outputs at this moment."

Pattern. Don't tune your scene's look against the preview tile. Tune it against the live render (Perform's main canvas, Author's live-preview pane in non-preview-tile mode). Use the preview tile as a visual table-of-contents.

docs.title: 3.7 Profile against the live runtime, not synthetic frames
docs.text:
The EV-PERF-BUDGETS work shipped a synthetic-workload bench harness for the engine subsystems, but the only honest signal for "does my scene hit 60 Hz" is the Perform top-bar FPS readout under your actual scene workload. Two posture rules:

  • Measure with audio active. A silent-mic test underestimates the analysis-thread cost; the scheduler tick that drains the audio snapshot is part of your per-frame budget.
  • Measure with the controls you intend to ship. A control that defaults to a cheap value (intensity = 0) hides cost that the operator will pay later when they dial it up. Sweep the controls through their declared range before declaring the scene shippable.

docs.title: 3.8 Cheap defaults, expensive worst cases
docs.text:
A useful sanity check: the cheapest possible state of your scene (all sliders at zero, all toggles off) should hit 60 Hz on an integrated GPU. The most expensive state (all sliders at max, all toggles on) should still degrade gracefully — drop to 30 Hz, not freeze.

If a particular control flips the scene from cheap to crash- expensive, that's a sign the control needs a clamp at the shader-author boundary, not the operator boundary. A raymarch_steps slider declared MAX = 200 is the operator choosing to render at 5 fps; declare MAX = 64 and let your shader's algorithmic budget do the right thing within that range.

docs.title: Chromaticity Uniform Reference
docs.text:
Every reactive uniform, script global and symbol Chromaticity exposes to scene authors uses the chroma_* namespace. Standard non-prefixed names (TIME, RENDERSIZE, the _Meta controls and the _* helper functions) complete the authoring surface.

Imported .synScene packages keep working: the importer and the live renderer translate their reference-format names onto the chroma_* names below automatically, so you never need to write them yourself.

docs.title: Live GPU UBO Layout (std140, binding 0)
docs.text:
In Chromaticity's live wgpu/Metal preview renderer (app/shell/src/render.rs), the runtime packs a single std140 uniform block at layout(set = 0, binding = 0). Native .chroma shaders declare the packed vec4 block directly:

layout(set = 0, binding = 0, std140) uniform ChromaUniforms {
    vec4 chroma_Time;       // x = elapsed_s, y = dt, z = frame, w = aspect
    vec4 chroma_Resolution; // x = width, y = height, z = 1/width, w = 1/height
    vec4 chroma_BPM;           // x = bpm, y = beat_time, z = on_beat, w = bpm_sin
    vec4 chroma_AudioRMS;   // x = rms
    vec4 chroma_AudioPeak;  // x = peak
    float chroma_AudioFFT[8]; // 8 log-spaced FFT bands (std140-padded array)
    vec4 chroma_Ctrl0;      // user controls 0..3
    vec4 chroma_Ctrl1;      // user controls 4..7
    vec4 chroma_Ctrl2;      // user controls 8..11
    vec4 chroma_Ctrl3;      // user controls 12..15 (including XY.y & script.js)
    // Optional extended reactive envelopes (appended when shader references chroma_AudioEnv0):
    vec4 chroma_AudioEnv0;  // x = level, y = hits, z = presence, w = time
    vec4 chroma_AudioEnv1;  // x = bass_level, y = bass_hits, z = bass_presence, w = bass_time
    vec4 chroma_AudioEnv2;  // x = mid_level, y = mid_hits, z = mid_presence, w = mid_time
    vec4 chroma_AudioEnv3;  // x = high_level, y = high_hits, z = high_presence, w = high_time
    vec4 chroma_AudioMeta;  // x = fade_in_out, y = intensity, z = bpm_confidence, w = random_on_beat
};

Note on extended envelopes: When a shader references chroma_AudioEnv0, the renderer automatically appends chroma_AudioEnv0..3 and chroma_AudioMeta to the binding-0 std140 buffer.

docs.title: Audio uniforms
docs.text: The audio analysis pipeline produces a per-tick AudioUniformSnapshot on the audio-analysis thread, which the audio-to-render adapter marshals into the GPU uniform slots above. Uniforms that read zero are the documented all-zero baseline for "no audio observed yet"; in Auto BPM mode, chroma_BPM.x reports 0.0 until audio tempo locks (or locks to the operator's manual tempo in Manual mode). The beat shapes (chroma_BPMTwitcher, chroma_BPMSin2/4/8, chroma_BPMTri/2/4/8) and the chroma_Spectrum sampler (backed by chroma_AudioFFT[8]) are currently computed live only for imported .synScene shaders; for native .chroma shaders they are planned (marked below).

docs.title: Scalar audio uniforms (runtime & planned catalog)
docs.text: Uniform Type Range Live GPU Status Description chroma_BPM vec4 (chroma_BPM.x) [50, 220] Live Estimated tempo (x=bpm, y=beat_time, z=on_beat, w=bpm_sin) chroma_BPMConfidence float (chroma_AudioMeta.z) [0, 1] Live Tempo-stability confidence; near 1 when the estimator agrees across the history window chroma_BPMTwitcher float [0, inf) Live (imported .synScene) / Planned (native .chroma) Exponential "jump" clock; floor is the beat count, fract is the per-beat twitch chroma_BPMSin float (chroma_BPM.w) [0, 1] Live Sine wave at BPM frequency, beat-phase-locked chroma_BPMSin2 float [0, 1] Live (imported .synScene) / Planned (native .chroma) Sine wave at BPM divided by 2 chroma_BPMSin4 float [0, 1] Live (imported .synScene) / Planned (native .chroma) Sine wave at BPM divided by 4 chroma_BPMTri float [0, 1] Live (imported .synScene) / Planned (native .chroma) Triangle wave at BPM frequency chroma_BPMTri2 float [0, 1] Live (imported .synScene) / Planned (native .chroma) Triangle wave at BPM divided by 2 chroma_BPMTri4 float [0, 1] Live (imported .synScene) / Planned (native .chroma) Triangle wave at BPM divided by 4 chroma_InputLevel float (chroma_AudioRMS.x) [0, inf) Live Pre-AGC instantaneous input level chroma_RawLevel float (chroma_AudioRMS.x) [0, inf) Live Alias of chroma_InputLevel with identical semantics chroma_Threshold float [0, 1] Runtime / OSC Operator-settable noise-floor gate; audio hops below this value publish zeroed chroma_Level* and chroma_*Hits chroma_AudioRMS vec4 (chroma_AudioRMS.x) [0, inf) Live Analysis-window root-mean-square energy of the mono-mixed audio frame chroma_AudioPeak vec4 (chroma_AudioPeak.x) [0, inf) Live Analysis-window peak magnitude of the mono-mixed audio frame

docs.text: Uniform Type Live GPU Status Description chroma_AudioFFT[8] float[8] Live (std140 binding 0) Eight log-spaced FFT band magnitudes covering 20 Hz to 20 kHz; element 0 is the lowest band, element 7 is the highest chroma_Spectrum sampler1D Live (imported .synScene) / Planned (native .chroma) Per-frame audio sampler (r=Raw FFT, g=Juiced, b=Smooth, a=Waveform); bridged from chroma_AudioFFT[8] on imported .synScene shaders chroma_LevelTrail sampler1D Planned Per-band historical levels over time, newest sample at u=0

docs.title: Time uniforms
docs.text: Uniform Type Description chroma_AudioTime float Audio-energy-integrated clock: advances faster when the music is louder (wall-clock time is chroma_Time.x) chroma_BassTime float Time accumulator that accelerates on bass-band hits chroma_MidTime float Time accumulator that accelerates on mid-band hits chroma_MidHighTime float Time accumulator that accelerates on mid-high-band hits chroma_HighTime float Time accumulator that accelerates on high-band hits chroma_CurvedTime float Same base as chroma_AudioTime with exponential acceleration on volume rises

docs.title: Authoring conventions
docs.text:
When a scene needs both raw analysis (the chroma_* audio primitives) and the smoothed / normalized parity surface (chroma_Level*, chroma_Spectrum), declare both uniforms; the binding adapter keeps the raw and smoothed paths independent so authors can pick the surface that matches each visual element. New uniforms and script outputs you define yourself can use any name; built-in reactive values always use chroma_*.

The published GLSL spelling for every uniform on this page is exactly the canonical name; the runtime does not perform per-binding casing fixups. A typo at the GLSL declaration site silently leaves the uniform unbound, which surfaces as a warning at scene load and as a zero-valued sample at render time.

Authored from engine/render/src/audio_adapter.rs (canonical UNIFORM_NAME_* constants), engine/audio/src/uniforms.rs (producer shape and band semantics), docs/36-reactive-symbol-catalog.md (reactive symbol catalog), and the docs/adr/ADR-019-audio-uniform-ipc-bridge.md IPC contract. The V1 hotkey map is read-only. Rebinding ships in V2 per the operator hotkey-map spec. The cap column on each row indicates whether the action is a free MVP capability or whether it requires an entitlement to fire; entitlement-gated rows fail closed when the matching capability is absent.

docs.title: Importing Shadertoy Scenes
docs.text: Chromaticity ships a one-way Shadertoy-to-.chroma converter that lets authors port single-pass Shadertoy fragments directly into the Chromaticity authoring environment. The converter wraps the Shadertoy body in a chromaticity-native shell, declares the canonical Shadertoy uniforms so the body code compiles unchanged, and emits a .chroma package that the runtime then loads through the standard scene pipeline.

docs.title: What the converter accepts
docs.text:
The input is a Shadertoy GLSL body containing:

void mainImage(out vec4 fragColor, in vec2 fragCoord) {
    // body
}

The converter wraps the body in a void main() entry that targets the naga GLSL frontend used by the engine's render path. The wrapper preamble declares the canonical Shadertoy-spelled uniforms so the imported body compiles without edits:

Uniform Purpose iTime Seconds since scene start iResolution Pixel size of the render target iTimeDelta Seconds since the previous frame iFrame Frame counter iMouse Mouse position and click state, Shadertoy-compatible

The runtime binding from these Shadertoy spellings to the canonical chromaticity-native reactive symbols (TIME, RENDERSIZE, …) is a binding-layer concern — the imported scene works in place without edits, and authors can migrate to the chromaticity-native symbols later if they want.

docs.title: What the converter rejects or warns on
docs.text:
The converter is strict about features it cannot represent in a single-pass mainImage shape. The rejection and warning surface is tagged with author-readable diagnostics:

  • VR mode (mainVR) — rejected; no plausible auto-mapping into a single-pass mainImage.
  • Cubemap entrypoint (mainCubemap) — surfaced as Warning::CubemapEntrypointDeferred; deferred to a future multipass-import pathway.
  • Webcam iChannel mapping — surfaced as Warning::WebcamIChannelDeferred; Chromaticity defers webcam binding to post-MVP. The body still compiles; the author can edit the .chroma package post-import to add a real binding.
  • Deprecated texture2D(...) calls — auto-corrected to texture(...) and surfaced as Warning::DeprecatedTexture2DAutoCorrected so the author has a trail of every machine-applied edit.

The converter is atomic: the caller sees either a fully-populated <scene_id>.chroma package or no package at all. Cleanup errors from a partially-written package are swallowed so the originating I/O cause stays surfaced in the diagnostics console.

docs.title: iChannel asset binding
docs.text:
Shadertoy scenes reference up to four iChannel0..iChannel3 slots backed by textures, cubemaps, video, audio, or the camera. The converter accepts a per-channel mapping at import time; each declared mapping causes the wrapper preamble to add a chromaticity-native binding-slot uniform (chroma_input_<channel>) and to rewrite the body's iChannelN references to that slot symbol before naga sees the source. Channels referenced by the body but not mapped at import emit Warning::MissingIChannelMapping so the author can either add the mapping in the converter and re-run, or edit the .chroma package post-import to bind the slot.

The shadertoy-fixtures/ subdirectory under <AppBundle>/Resources/scenes/ ships the iChannel asset corpus the import tests draw from — see Library Workflow for how that subdirectory is excluded from the launchable scene set.

docs.title: After import
docs.text: The output is a .chroma package matching the same on-disk shape that the in-app scaffolder produces. Once written, the package surfaces in the library through the standard discovery path and is loadable through the standard scene pipeline described in Scene Workflow. Imported scenes carry the format tag shadertoy-v1-import so the operator can filter them in the library browser.

docs.title: What is not imported
docs.text:
The Shadertoy import path is intentionally narrow:

  • ISF scenes — imported through a separate ISF-import path that is currently a reject-with-diagnostic surface; native ISF execution is deferred to V2.
  • Multi-buffer Shadertoy compositions — out of scope for the V1 import; the multipass-import pathway is a future-wave ADR.
  • Sound shaders — Chromaticity is a visual runtime; Shadertoy sound-shader bodies are rejected.

docs.title: Capability gating
docs.text: Shadertoy import is gated by the authoring.import capability. With no entitlement token present, the import action is disabled in the operator HUD with the standard locked-row affordance; see Settings Reference for the entitlement model.

docs.title: Library Workflow
docs.text: The Chromaticity library is the operator's home for browsing, searching, and launching scenes. It indexes scenes from three disjoint sources and presents them through one logical browser.

docs.title: Scene sources
docs.text:
The library merges three sources into a single result set:

  • Bundled scenes — read-only packages shipped inside the application bundle under <AppBundle>/Resources/scenes/.
  • User scenes — scenes under the active user-data scenes folder (<UserDataRoot>/Scenes/). Operators may register additional folders through Settings; results merge into the same logical library.
  • Author workspace — scenes currently open in the in-app authoring environment.

docs.title: Bundled scenes — the four-subdirectory taxonomy
docs.text:
The bundled scene root is exactly the four subdirectories named below. Discovery never walks any other path under the bundle's Resources/:

Subdirectory Purpose welcome/ Single-package first-launch onboarding scene library/ Full Chromaticity-original clean-room corpus examples/ Minimal demonstration scenes for each authoring feature (multi-pass, script, transitions, media, audio-reactive) shadertoy-fixtures/ iChannel asset fixtures consumed by Shadertoy import — not user-launchable scenes

The shadertoy-fixtures/ subdirectory is intentionally excluded from the launcher; its contents back the import path described in Scene Workflow.

docs.title: Per-scene metadata
docs.text:
Each scene exposes the following metadata to the library browser, drawn from scene.json and the package's filesystem state:

  • TITLE — display name; falls back to the package directory name when absent.
  • CREDIT — author attribution.
  • DESCRIPTION — short prose summary, surfaced in the detail pane.
  • IMAGE_PATH — relative path to the canonical thumbnail; see the thumbnail-fallback chain below.
  • TAGS and legacy CATEGORIES — searchable / filterable token lists.
  • Package path, last-modified time, scene-format tag.

The format tag is one of native-chroma-scene, compat-syn-scene, shadertoy-v1-import, or isf-import. Format tags are catalog-only — they are distinct from the runtime compatibility profile each scene also carries (compat-syn-v1 or native-chroma-v1).

docs.title: Thumbnails
docs.text:
When a scene declares an explicit IMAGE_PATH, the library loads it directly. Otherwise the loader walks a deterministic fallback chain:

  1. <package>/<package_stem>.png (matching the package directory name).
  2. An auto-generated preview captured at frame 60 with default audio-silent state.
  3. A format-family fallback icon shipped under <AppBundle>/Resources/thumbnails/ — one per scene-format tag.

Thumbnails regenerate on operator request through the scene context menu and are captured with a deterministic seeded RNG so re-renders match across runs.

docs.title: Browser capabilities
docs.text:
The library view supports both grid and list presentation. From either:

  • Full-text search across TITLE, CREDIT, DESCRIPTION, TAGS, and CATEGORIES.
  • Filter by compat profile, by tag, by presence of script.js, by presence of bundled media.
  • Sort by title, credit, last-modified, tag relevance, or author-defined order.
  • Drag a scene into the playlist editor from any view.
  • Keyboard navigation — arrow keys move the selection, Enter launches the selected scene, Shift+Enter launches with a preset prompt. See Hotkey Reference for the full vocabulary.

docs.title: Launching a scene
docs.text:
Single-click selects a scene; double-click or Enter launches it. The launch target depends on the active transport mode:

  • In playlist mode, launching a scene replaces the active playlist slot and follows the slot's transition descriptor.
  • In instant-scene mode, launching cuts directly to the scene with the operator's chosen transition.

Optional preset launch (Shift+Enter) prompts for a Snap-slot name; the default Snap is slot zero ("gold preset"). Snap slots are the operator-facing name for per-scene quick-recall presets — see the Hotkey Reference for the keyboard mappings and OSC Routes for the wire-level surface (where the literal favslots is retained for compat-syn-v1 compatibility).

docs.title: Indexing posture
docs.text: Library discovery is filesystem-backed. The indexer rescans on operator request and on filesystem-change events; for large user-scene folders, the rescan is incremental against the cached prior index. The search and filter surface in the operator HUD reads from this index over in-process IPC, not from a re-walk of disk on every keystroke.

docs.title: Livestreaming Chromaticity
docs.text: This page documents the operator pathway for routing the Chromaticity render output into a livestreaming application such as OBS Studio, and covers what is wired today, what is scaffolded but not yet operational, and what is planned. Livestream pathing depends on a frame-publishing back end (Syphon on macOS, Spout on Windows, NDI cross-platform); several of those back ends are partial or future-wave work at the time of writing.

docs.title: Direct Twitch RTMPS Broadcasting (Wired Today)
docs.text: Chromaticity ships built-in Twitch RTMPS/RTMP live broadcasting directly from the Mix deck (LiveBroadcast controls) using hardware-accelerated h264_videotoolbox (macOS) or libx264 via host ffmpeg, with automatic stream-key redaction and live audio capture on macOS. You can broadcast your multi-layer Mix composite (GPU shaders, webcam, local video/images, YouTube stream-in, and text overlays) straight to Twitch without needing OBS in between.

docs.title: External Frame-Sharing Bridges (Syphon / Spout / NDI)
docs.text:
External GPU frame-sharing publish is not operational yet. Chromaticity ships the Syphon adapter scaffold and the engine-side bridge, but the publish_syphon_output real implementation is a Wave 1c-β follow-up that has not landed. Operators who attempt to add a Syphon Client source in OBS today will not see a Chromaticity server on the bus, because the chromaticity output adapter does not yet hand wgpu-rendered textures into the framework's publishFrameTexture: call site.

This page captures the recipe operators will follow once that real-impl lands. The directory + receiver scaffolding, the error taxonomy, the operator-facing health surface, and the engine bridge are all in place; what remains is the wgpu ↔ IOSurface extraction plumbing on the publish side. The receiver side (consuming a Syphon feed from another macOS app into Chromaticity as a video input) is also scaffold-complete pending the same hardware-validation pass.

For the current state of the underlying integration work, see the "Wave 1c-β follow-ups" section in the repository's project memory. The honest follow-ups list at the bottom of this page tracks the remaining work items.

docs.title: macOS — Syphon
docs.text:
The Syphon I/O adapter (integrations/syphon-adapter/) compiles on macOS and exposes the public surface locked by ADR-021:

  • SyphonInputAdapter — for consuming frames published by other macOS apps on the Syphon bus into Chromaticity as a video input. Polling-consume model: the engine scheduler-tick pulls the most recent frame each tick; backlog frames are dropped on saturation.
  • SyphonOutputAdapter — for publishing Chromaticity's render output to the bus. The type-shape contract (bind / unbind / publish / health) is wired; the framework-side publishFrameTexture:onCommandBuffer:imageRegion:flipped: call site is the deferred follow-up.
  • SyphonServerDirectory — singleton discovery surface keyed off the SyphonServerDirectory.sharedDirectory Objective-C class method. The NSDistributedNotificationCenter observer that fires on server-add / server-update / server-remove notifications is a carried-forward follow-up; the directory snapshot path (initial enumeration) is wired.
  • Texture binding namespace — input feeds bind under the chroma_SyphonInput[N] uniform namespace on the engine side; output servers register under an operator-overridable name template.

The texture pixel format is locked to BGRA8Unorm, which is the universally-supported format across Syphon consumers including OBS's Syphon plugin, Resolume, Madmapper, and VDMX.

docs.title: macOS — what OBS will see
docs.text: Once the publish_syphon_output real-impl lands, OBS Studio with the Syphon plugin installed will list "Chromaticity" (or the operator- chosen name) under Add Source → Syphon Client. The plugin reads the same SyphonServerDirectory Chromaticity registers against; no additional wiring is required on the OBS side.

docs.title: Windows + cross-platform — current state
docs.text:
• Spout (Windows): not yet integrated. The adapter does not exist; a future PR will add it under integrations/spout-adapter/. The cross-platform parity bring-up is tracked as a Wave 1c-β follow-up cluster sibling of the Syphon publish work.
  • NDI (cross-platform): scaffolded only. NDI is referenced in the planning corpus as the macOS-and-Windows fallback for operators who cannot route through Syphon or Spout, but no adapter crate exists yet.
  • Virtual webcam output (cross-platform): not planned for MVP. Operators on a single workstation should prefer Syphon (macOS) or Spout (Windows) once those ship; cross-machine routing should prefer NDI.

docs.title: Operator pathway — forward-looking recipe
docs.text: The recipe below describes how operators will livestream Chromaticity once the publish path lands. Until then, treat the workflow as a preview of the intended operator flow; the commands and UI surfaces named here may shift in detail.

docs.title: 1. Install OBS Studio (macOS)
docs.text:
1. Install OBS Studio (28.0 or later recommended; OBS Studio 33+ ships built-in macOS Syphon support via mac-syphon.plugin under Sources → Add → Syphon Client — no third-party Syphon plugin needed).

On Windows the equivalent will be the Spout plugin for OBS once Chromaticity's Spout adapter lands; the configuration steps below will map across with the source type renamed from "Syphon Client" to "Spout".

docs.title: 2. Configure audio capture
docs.text: On macOS, Chromaticity captures system audio (including Rekordbox 7 PC MASTER OUT) directly via zero-install Core Audio Process Tap (ADR-022), with no BlackHole or virtual loopback driver required. On Windows/Linux, or when routing into OBS alongside Chromaticity, you can optionally use WASAPI loopback or a virtual cable (BlackHole / Loopback / VB-Cable). For audio-reactivity setup details, see the Audio Reactivity page.

docs.title: 3. Enable the Syphon output in Chromaticity
docs.text:
Once the publish path lands, the Settings → Output tab will expose a Syphon Server toggle and an operator-overridable server name. The default name follows the DEFAULT_OUTPUT_NAME_TEMPLATE constant in the adapter (a predictable template the operator can override per show). With the toggle enabled, the SyphonServerDirectory will advertise "Chromaticity" (or the chosen name) on the bus immediately; OBS will pick it up without restart.

The output adapter exposes an operator-facing health surface mirroring the camera adapter's health model — Bound, Disconnected, Negotiating, or Faulted with an operator-readable diagnostic. The TopBar adapter pills already render an OUT indicator that will read this health value once wired; see the Perform Mode page for the adapter-pill model.

docs.title: 4. Add the Syphon Client source in OBS
docs.text:
In OBS Studio:

  1. Click the + button under the Sources panel.
  2. Choose Syphon Client.
  3. Give the source a name (this is OBS's internal label, separate from the Chromaticity server name).
  4. In the source properties, the Source dropdown will list every Syphon server currently on the bus. Pick the Chromaticity server.
  5. Confirm the preview pane shows live Chromaticity output.

Resolution, frame rate, and color space are negotiated through the underlying IOSurface (BGRA8Unorm; the resolution matches the Chromaticity render target). No additional configuration is required.

docs.title: 5. Confirm audio sync and round-trip latency
docs.text:
Both video (Chromaticity → Syphon → OBS) and audio (system → loopback → OBS) flow into OBS as independent sources. Audio sync is the operator's responsibility:

  • In OBS, right-click the audio source and choose Advanced Audio Properties. The Sync Offset column shifts audio relative to video in milliseconds (positive values delay audio).
  • A reasonable starting offset is 0 ms; tune by ear against beat- reactive scenes. Syphon adds negligible video latency (sub-millisecond on modern Apple Silicon); the loopback audio path is typically near-zero.

docs.title: 6. Stream key configuration and bitrate
docs.text: When broadcasting directly from Chromaticity's Mix deck, Twitch RTMPS/RTMP ingest URLs, redacted stream keys, resolution, FPS, and bitrate are configured directly in Chromaticity's Live Broadcast drawer. When using an external encoder such as OBS Studio, those settings remain in OBS's Settings → Stream and Settings → Output tabs.

docs.title: Audio capture posture
docs.text: On macOS, Chromaticity supports zero-install Core Audio Process Tap system-audio capture (ADR-022) as well as multi-channel DJ controller Master-vs-Cue stereo-pair isolation (DDJ-FLX10, DJM-A9), so you do not need BlackHole or a kernel audio driver to drive audio-reactive visuals or broadcast audio. On Windows/Linux, or when sharing audio with external tools like OBS Studio, you can select any host input or virtual loopback device in Settings → Audio.
