docs.title: OSC Route Reference
docs.text: Chromaticity exposes Open Sound Control (OSC) inbound and outbound routes for show-control automation and external surface integration. This page enumerates the canonical route taxonomy honoured by the OSC adapter at the top-level prefixes the slice-2 route schema declares.

docs.title: Defaults and discovery
docs.text:
By default the OSC adapter binds the inbound listener to the loopback interface (127.0.0.1) and treats the outbound target as loopback until the operator configures a routable address. Exposing the inbound listener on a routable interface is an explicit operator opt-in. The operator can confirm the bound interface and current rate-limit posture through the AdapterPill chrome at the top of any view.

Two payload-hardening defaults are pinned by the network adapter:

  • The maximum accepted OSC packet size is 64 KiB. Oversize packets are rejected with an osc-malformed-class diagnostic and no state mutation.
  • The maximum nested OSC bundle depth is 4. Deeper payloads are rejected for the same reason.

Per-route inbound traffic is rate-limited at a default ceiling of 100 messages per second per (adapter, route) pair. Over-rate messages are dropped with an osc-rate-limited diagnostic emitted no more than once per second per route to prevent the diagnostics channel itself from saturating.

docs.title: Top-level prefixes
docs.text:
The slice-2 route schema declares four canonical top-level prefixes; addresses outside this set are rejected at parse time.

Prefix Purpose /controls Scene-author parameter control (control-bank reads and writes) /scenes Scene-selection and scene-launch routes /audio Audio-pipeline routes (threshold, level discovery) /render Render-loop and resolution control

Companion route families used by the operator hotkey vocabulary (/playlist, /playlists, /favslots, /presets) are part of the broader IO surface specified in the integrations document; see the plurality and alias rules below.

docs.title: Scene routes
docs.text:
Route Direction Args Description /scenes outbound (list payload) Library scene-name listing emitted on bind and on library-change /scenes/{name} {preset?} inbound scene name; optional preset name Launch scene; unsupplied preset resolves to Snap 0 / gold /scenes/{name} outbound scene name Scene-change announcement emitted on every cut or transition completion

The legacy singular-root forms /scene/{name} and /scene/{name} {preset} are accepted as compat-syn-v1 aliases. Outbound emission during the dual-emit window publishes both the canonical plural form and the singular alias.

docs.title: Snap (favslots) routes
docs.text:
Snap is the operator-facing name for per-scene quick-recall slots; the wire-level literal favslots is retained under compat-syn-v1 for compatibility.

Route Direction Args Description /favslots/{n} inbound (apply) slot index n in [0, 15] Recall Snap slot n for the current scene /favslots/{n}/save inbound (save) slot index n Overwrite Snap slot n with the current state /favslots/{n}/clear inbound (clear) slot index n Delete Snap slot n; the slot returns to unbound /favslots/{n}/name {string} outbound slot index, name string Snap-slot name announcement on show load and after any save or clear

The apply / save / clear distinction is wire-level explicit through the route suffix; there is no implicit mode selection from message arguments. The legacy /favslots/{n} {mode} form with a string argument of "apply", "save", or "clear" is accepted as a compat-syn-v1 alias.

docs.title: Playlist routes
docs.text:
Route Direction Args Description /playlists outbound (list payload) Show-playlist listing on bind /playlists/next inbound (none) Advance to next scene in playlist /playlists/previous inbound (none) Step back to previous scene in playlist /playlists/position {i} inbound and outbound integer index; negative counts from end Jump to absolute playlist position (inbound); emitted on every position change (outbound) /playlists/play inbound (none) Resume playlist transport /playlists/toggleplay inbound (none) Toggle playlist play / pause /playlists/select {name} inbound playlist name Select a named playlist as the active one /playlists/current {name} outbound active playlist name Emitted on playlist change

The /playlists/position {i} route is bidirectional: sending an integer index jumps the playlist to that position, where negative values count from the end (-1 is the last scene, -2 the second-to-last, etc.); outbound emission follows every position change so show-control surfaces and external recorders receive a running position stream without needing to track /playlists/next transitions manually.

The singular-root action forms /playlist/next, /playlist/previous, /playlist/toggleplay are accepted as compat-syn-v1 aliases for the plural-root canonical forms. The hotkey overlay surfaces these singular forms in its OSC column for compatibility with reference scenes.

docs.title: Render routes
docs.text:
Route Direction Args Description /render/enabled {0|1} inbound flag Toggle the render loop on or off; the GPU scheduler halts scene rendering while UI and adapter threads stay responsive /render/resolution {w} {h} inbound width, height Resize the render output surface (capability-gated render.custom-resolution) /render/fps {float} inbound target FPS Override the render FPS target

/render/enabled 0 is non-destructive: outbound audio, MIDI, and OSC state continue to publish, and shader pipelines remain warm so the restoration frame on /render/enabled 1 is within one frame budget. Useful for SMPTE-slaved setups, A/V calibration, and operator-triggered "hold current output" cues.

docs.title: Audio routes
docs.text:
Route Direction Args Description /audio/threshold {float} inbound and outbound clamped to [0, 1] Set or announce the audio noise-floor gate; updates chroma_AudioRMS-based gate within one audio hop /audio/threshold/sample inbound (none) Sample the current 200 ms rolling RMS of the audio level and set the threshold to that value; emits /audio/threshold {float} outbound on completion

The /audio/threshold route is bidirectional: inbound messages set the noise-floor gate level and the engine emits the current threshold value outbound after each change so external controllers stay in sync. An outbound emission is also sent on adapter bind so listeners initialise their display to the current threshold without needing an explicit poll.

Audio hops with RMS below the threshold publish zeroed level and hit family uniforms; the threshold is the operator's primary tool for rejecting room noise and HVAC bleed.

docs.title: Compat dual-emit window
docs.text:
Chromaticity's outbound sender supports a dual-emit migration window for operators who need to run legacy show controllers subscribed to the Synesthesia-compat singular-root address forms (/scene/{name}, /preset/{name}, /playlist/next, etc.) alongside new controllers subscribed to the canonical plural-root forms.

When dual_emit_enabled = true (operator opt-in; off by default) the sender emits each outbound message twice: once on the canonical address and once on the compat-syn-v1 alias address. The canonical emission has priority — if the outbound socket is momentarily congested the alias datagram is skipped rather than delaying the canonical one.

An optional RFC 3339 deadline (dual_emit_until) can be configured so the migration window closes automatically on a specific date without needing a manual operator toggle. When dual_emit_until is set and the deadline has passed, dual-emit is inactive regardless of the dual_emit_enabled flag.

The compat alias emits counter in the OSC view's Adapter section shows how many alias datagrams have been sent since the adapter was started. A zero counter with dual-emit enabled means no outbound messages have been sent yet; a rising counter confirms legacy controllers are receiving the compat-form addresses.

To enable the dual-emit window from the OSC view, toggle the dual-emit switch in the Operator settings panel and confirm the counter begins rising when a scene loads or a control changes.

docs.title: Controls routes
docs.text: The /controls namespace is the runtime parameter-write surface used by external surfaces (TouchOSC, MIDI-to-OSC bridges, custom show runners). The canonical shape is /controls/{bank}/{control} followed by a typed value argument; the slice-2 router parses these into a canonical segment vector for the slice-3 dispatch surface that lands the typed-command translation. Author-side scenes declare their expected control bank in the scene script; the runtime rejects writes to unknown banks with a route-mismatch diagnostic.

docs.title: Plurality convention
docs.text:
The collection roots use the plural form (/scenes, /presets, /playlists, /favslots, /controls); action verbs and listing queries live under the collection root. Chromaticity V1 canonical form is plural-root throughout inbound and outbound emission. The singular reference-app forms (/scene/{name}, /preset/{name}, /playlist/next) are accepted as compat-syn-v1 aliases.

Authored from integrations/osc-adapter/src/routes.rs (slice-2 route-prefix taxonomy) and integrations/osc-adapter/src/defaults.rs (network defaults), against docs/adr/ADR-013-networking-defaults-and-security.md and the docs/08-io-integrations.md OSC sections. Clean-room per docs/29-cleanroom-legal-policy-baseline.md.

docs.title: Perform Mode
docs.text: Perform mode is the operator's main runtime surface during a show. It arranges live scene controls, the meta colour pipeline, the media strip, the preview hero, the audio-reactivity panel, and the scene rail into a single dense layout that is reachable without opening nested panels.

docs.title: The five panels
docs.text:
The Perform view is laid out across three columns:

Column Panels Left Scene Controls, Meta Controls, Media Strip Middle Preview hero, Audio Reactivity panel Right Scene rail with Perform / Edit toggle, Setlist selector, Prev / Next / Shuffle row, scrollable scene list

Every interactive element on the surface is reachable through both mouse and keyboard.

docs.title: Scene Controls
docs.text:
The Scene Controls panel surfaces every author-declared control for the currently active scene as a typed widget — sliders for numeric parameters, toggles for booleans, swatches for colours, and combo selectors for enumerations. Each control row carries a per-control hotkey-hint badge; while a control has keyboard focus, the control-focused hotkeys take effect:

Key Action D Set the focused control to its default value R Set the focused control to a random value in its range P Set the focused control to its value in the active preset L Toggle the lock state (the locked control ignores randomisation)

The full operator hotkey vocabulary lives at Hotkey Reference.

docs.title: Meta Controls
docs.text: The Meta Controls panel exposes the scene-agnostic colour and transform pipeline. A live Rust post-pass (app/shell/src/commands/render.rs::apply_meta_color_pass) applies the nine active controls — invert, brightness, gamma, contrast, hue, saturation, vert mirror, hor mirror, and limit colors — directly to render_gpu_frame, so the adjustments carry through to both the Perform preview and stage output. Dedicated GPU shader _Meta* uniforms and custom duotone swatch anchors remain planned for a future render pass. The hotkeys M / B / G / C / H / Y enter modal slider-adjust mode against the matching meta control; Esc exits.

docs.title: The Preview hero
docs.text: The Preview hero shows the live render output. It mirrors the actual output surface so the operator sees exactly what the audience sees. Beneath the preview, the Audio Reactivity panel surfaces the live audio uniforms — four named band tiles, the BPM strip, and the FFT visualiser.

docs.title: The Scene rail
docs.text:
The right-column scene rail surfaces:

  • A four-button rail to switch between Scenes / Presets / Edit / Add modes.
  • A Perform / Edit toggle that gates the Author surface (Edit mode is capability-gated by authoring.edit).
  • A Setlist selector pinning the active playlist.
  • A Prev / Next / Shuffle row mirroring the playlist transport hotkeys (<- / -> / Space).
  • A scrollable list of every scene in the active setlist, with the current scene highlighted.

docs.title: The Snap bar
docs.text:
A Snap bar persists across the bottom of Perform mode: ten quick-recall slots, addressed by 1 through 0 in operator focus. Saving uses Shift+1 through Shift+0; clearing uses Alt+Shift+1 through Alt+Shift+0. Slot zero is the "gold preset" and is recallable through Cmd+0 / Ctrl+0 as a guaranteed safe state.

The Snap surface is the chromaticity-native naming for what the compat-syn-v1 OSC routes still call favslots — see OSC Routes for the wire-level mapping.

docs.title: TopBar adapter pills
docs.text:
The persistent TopBar HUD across the top of Chromaticity renders live status pills for the active runtime surfaces — OUT, AUDIO, MIDI, and OSC (camera and Syphon pills are not surfaced in the HUD yet). Each pill surfaces:

  • A connectivity dot (online / degraded / offline).
  • The active target, device, or port state.
  • A click target opening the corresponding inspector or settings view.

When an adapter is degraded, a one-line banner appears at the top of the view explaining the cause and pointing at Settings for the recovery action.

docs.title: Why Perform mode is the default
docs.text: Perform mode is the surface every operator hits first because it balances density with safety: every common live action is reachable without nesting, and the destructive actions (Snap clear, scene delete) require either a confirmation prompt or a modifier. The Author and Library views are routed under their own sidebar entries for the iteration loops where density beats safety the other way around.

docs.title: Quickstart — first-launch recipe
docs.text:
This page walks a brand-new operator from "I just installed Chromaticity" to "I have an audio-reactive scene running and I'm dragging a control to confirm it reacts." Allow ten to fifteen minutes end-to-end.

The recipe is honest about which surfaces are live in production today and which are scheduled follow-ups. Where the engine is still synthetic or partially wired, the page calls that out plainly rather than pretending the final surface is in place. The companion [Pre-Alpha Smoke Checklist][smoke] in the release-eng tree carries the exhaustive verification matrix; this page is the operator-facing narrative.

docs.title: 1. First launch — the Welcome view
docs.text:
When Chromaticity opens for the first time it routes to Welcome. You see a centred hero with three quick-start cards:

  • Quick Start — routes to the Library view so you can pick a bundled scene.
  • Import Setlist — disabled today. The Import view ports in a later wave; the card is reserved for that surface.
  • Empty Project — routes to the Perform view with a blank scene loaded.

Underneath the cards is a hint row: "Audio input required · MIDI optional · Ableton Link supported." The first two are accurate today; the Link tagline is reserved for future work.

The sidebar rail along the left edge surfaces the rest of the app — Perform, Library, Author, Playlist, Media, MIDI, OSC, Audio, Patch, Onboard, Settings, Help. Each rail icon shows a tooltip on hover. The status bar across the bottom carries the active tier badge, adapter state pills, and the theme name.

!!! note "If the bundled Library looks empty"

On a fresh install where the Tauri bundle's `bundle.resources` widening
has not yet landed (this widens the bundled scene corpus into the app
package), the Library may show no built-in scenes. The clean-room
corpus exists under `engine/scene/tests/fixtures/scenes/` in the
repository; once the resources path widens, the Library auto-
discovers them. Until that lands, point Settings → Storage at your
own scene folder to populate the grid.

docs.title: 2. Audio setup
docs.text: Chromaticity is an audio-reactive runtime. The audio path is live in production via the Wave 1c-α-2 cross-seam wiring: the producer thread in engine/audio publishes a per-tick analysis snapshot; the scheduler emits the snapshot over IPC to the UI at sixty hertz; the four named band tiles and BPM strip in the AudioReactivity widget read the live snapshot end-to-end.

docs.title: Pick the input device
docs.text:
Open Settings → Audio Device. The Input Device dropdown enumerates host audio devices through the audio adapter's input picker. Pick the device you want the analysis pipeline to read from. The picker persists across restarts through the TOML-backed Settings store under Tauri's app_data_dir.

The dropdown's selection takes effect when the analysis thread next restarts — typically the next scene load. The thread does not hot-swap devices mid-show to keep the snapshot pipeline deterministic.

docs.title: macOS — capturing system audio
docs.text:
The producer uses cpal's default input device on macOS, which means the microphone, not system audio output. macOS doesn't expose system-output capture through standard audio APIs. The operator has three paths:

Easy path — acoustic mic pickup. Play music on your computer speakers and let the built-in microphone hear it. Clap or speak near the mic to confirm the named band tiles respond.

Cleaner path — virtual loopback. Install a virtual audio device that routes system output to a virtual input:

# BlackHole (free, MIT-licensed) — install with Homebrew:
brew install blackhole-2ch

# or grab the installer from existential.audio/blackhole/

After installing BlackHole, configure macOS to send system audio to it (Audio MIDI Setup → create a Multi-Output Device that includes your speakers and BlackHole, then route system output there). Restart Chromaticity, open Settings → Audio Device, and pick BlackHole 2ch in the Input Device dropdown. Loopback (paid, more flexible) is the GUI-driven alternative.

No-mic path — silent fallback. If the machine has no input device at all, the producer falls back to a silent source and emits all-zero snapshots. The visualizer widgets stay on synthetic fallback; that is expected behaviour, not a bug.

docs.title: Windows — capturing system audio
docs.text: Windows operators use VB-Cable (free) or VoiceMeeter (free, heavier GUI). Install VB-Cable, set your default playback device to "CABLE Input", set Chromaticity's input device in Settings to "CABLE Output", and audio routed to system playback is captured by the analysis pipeline.

docs.title: Confirm the device is producing signal
docs.text:
Open the Audio view. The live monitoring meter at the top of the view shows the input level in real time; if you see motion when audio is playing, the device is producing signal and the analysis pipeline is reading it.

The first ~1.2 seconds after the audio pipeline starts is a documented warming window — the BpmRing, BeatDots, and band tiles render in a dimmed placeholder state while the FFT and BPM accumulators fill. Once the analysis window is full, the widgets transition to live values. The new top-bar AUDIO pill reflects the transition: yellow during warming, green when ready, red on a producer-thread fault.

docs.title: 3. Load your first scene
docs.text:
Open the Library view from the sidebar (or click Quick Start on the Welcome card). The library merges three sources: bundled scenes shipped inside the app bundle, user scenes under your registered storage folders, and the active Author workspace. See Library Workflow for the full source taxonomy.

Scenes are arranged as a card grid. Each card shows a thumbnail (canvas-2d procedural — see the honesty note below), a title, a source pill, and a few tag chips. Single-click any card to surface its detail in the right-pane sidebar with a <SceneCanvas> preview, the description, credit, and the controls-count badge. Double-click — or hit Enter on a focused card — to load the scene into the runtime.

The four bundled welcome scenes you'll see first:

  • welcome.chroma — gradient-drift backdrop with three controls (intro_scale, drift_speed, accent). The first-launch onboarding scene per the scene library spec.
  • quick-start.chroma — minimal four-control scene combining a brightness slider, a contrast knob, a saturation slider, and a tint color. Sweep every primary widget kind in one place.
  • controls-tour.chroma — comprehensive widget showcase exercising every input kind the Inspector can render (slider, knob, toggle, color, xy, dropdown).
  • first-cue.chroma — single-cue starter scene illustrating a fade-driven transition from calm baseline to emphasis. Useful when you want to feel how cues drive control values.

After loading, the app routes to Perform. The Scene Controls header binds to the loaded scene's NAME and the Scene Controls plus Meta Controls panels render against the loaded control schema.

!!! warning "Preview is canvas-2d procedural, not live GPU render"

The Perform preview pane and every `<SceneCanvas>` instance render
through a canvas-2d procedural adapter — sixteen built-in scene
"kinds" mapped from each scene's metadata (kaleido, rings, plasma,
orbit, tunnel, fluid, lattice, bars, and friends). The live GPU
render pipeline is ADR-011 Phase-2-plus deferred. Dragging a
control fires the dispatch through to the engine and the engine
commits the value — that path is live — but what you see in the
preview is the procedural visualisation, not the actual GLSL
output. The procedural preview is wireframe-faithful for
structural feedback (rotation, warp, audio reactivity); it is not
the final rendered image.

docs.title: 4. Drag a control
docs.text:
In Perform, look at the Scene Controls panel along the left column. Each control row is a typed widget — sliders for numeric parameters, knobs for tighter-range numerics, toggles for booleans, swatches for colours. Each row carries a per-control hotkey-hint badge along its trailing edge.

Drag a Fader. Three things happen in order:

  1. The widget's local drag position moves under your pointer.
  2. The dispatch through set_control IPC fires.
  3. The engine commits the value through its command bus and returns it; the widget snaps to the engine-committed value (which, for un-clamped controls, equals what you dragged to).

If the control name maps to one of the renderer's known pre-multiplier axes — speed, intensity, tint, rotation_speed, warp_amount, invert, mirror — the canvas-2d procedural preview responds visibly. The Wave 2.8/2.9 SC.A widening added the pulse(lvl) = 0.6 + lvl * 0.4 coupling envelope so the procedural visuals couple to the live audio level (sixty percent intensity at silent audio, full intensity at peak).

Controls whose names are NOT in the renderer's known set still fire the engine dispatch correctly but produce no visible change in the preview. Those controls render with a data-preview-wired="false" affordance — the row dims to seventy percent opacity and a hover tooltip explains: "engine-only — preview adapter not implemented." That is the honest signal that the engine sees the value but the canvas-2d preview adapter has no visualisation for that name. The GPU render pipeline (ADR-011 Phase-2-plus) is where those controls will land their visible effect.

docs.title: Quick action buttons
docs.text:
Above each control panel sit three action buttons that operate on the whole panel at once:

  • Default — resets every control in the panel to its declared default.
  • Random — randomises every control to a value in its declared range. Locked rows are skipped.
  • Lock-all — toggles a per-row lock on every control in the panel. Locked rows dim and short-circuit the dispatch so the engine never sees suppressed values.

Per-row locks also expose the L hotkey while the row has focus; D sets the focused control to default; R randomises it; P sets it to its value in the active preset. See Hotkey Reference for the full vocabulary.

docs.title: 5. Try Perform mode
docs.text: You're already in Perform after loading the scene. A few things to exercise.

docs.title: STANDARD versus CONSOLE variant
docs.text: The top bar carries a STANDARD / CONSOLE toggle. STANDARD is the classic two-column layout — Scene Controls and Meta Controls on the left, Preview hero and Audio Reactivity panel in the middle, scene rail on the right. CONSOLE collapses to a denser three-column layout intended for operators who want more density at the cost of breathing room. The choice persists per launch.

docs.title: Snap recall
docs.text:
The Snap bar runs across the bottom of Perform with eight quick-recall slots. Slots are addressed by the number keys 1 through 8 in operator focus, plus a "gold preset" recallable through Cmd+0 or Ctrl+0 as the guaranteed safe state.

  • Click slot N — recalls the saved state.
  • Cmd+click slot N (macOS) / Ctrl+click slot N (Windows) — saves the current control state into slot N.
  • Alt+click slot N — clears the slot.
  • Right-click slot N — opens an inline rename input for a custom label ("Intro" / "Drop" / "Outro"). Labels persist across restarts through localStorage.

Try it: drag a Fader, Cmd-click slot 1 to save, drag the Fader elsewhere, click slot 1 to ping back to the saved state.

docs.title: Preset and playlist transport
docs.text:
The right-column scene rail carries a Prev / Next / Shuffle row that mirrors playlist transport. Click Next to advance one slot; click Previous to step back. The preset rail above it lets you click a preset to recall it; Cmd-click an empty preset slot to save the current control state to it (in-process snapshot — see the honesty note).

!!! warning "Shuffle advances by +1, not random"

The engine does not yet carry a shuffle command. The Perform
Shuffle button advances by +1 like Next; the label parity with
the bundle is preserved but the ordering is not randomised.
A future-wave engine `Command::Shuffle` widening is on the
follow-up list.

!!! note "Preset save is in-process only"

Cmd-click preset save captures the current control state into an
in-memory preset bank. Settings-TOML disk persistence is a
deferred follow-up; quit and relaunch will not restore the saved
preset.

docs.title: 6. Confirm audio reactivity
docs.text:
Make sure your audio source is playing (music near the mic, or system-output routed through BlackHole / VB-Cable). Watch the top-bar HUD and the Audio Reactivity panel below the preview hero.

  • The VU meter in the top bar pulses with the live RMS.
  • The BpmRing rotates phase-locked to the estimated tempo.
  • The BeatDots strip flashes on each beat boundary.
  • The Audio Reactivity panel's four named band tiles ("bass" / "low-mid" / "mid" / "high") move in proportion to the spectrum energy in each band. The BPM strip beneath them tracks the live BPM.

The four named tiles are derived from the engine's eight log-spaced FFT bands via a documented pairwise average — see Audio Reactivity for the reduction formula and the full uniform catalog.

!!! note "Some audio surfaces stay synthetic"

The forty-eight bar FFT visualizer inside the Audio Reactivity
panel and the inline sixty-four bar Spectrum surface in the Audio
Uniforms view both stay synthetic-driven in the V1 release. They
paint a deterministic visual placeholder, not the live FFT — that
retrofit is post-MVP UX work. The four named band tiles and the
BPM strip are the live-driven surfaces today.

docs.title: Set the noise-floor threshold
docs.text:
If you're in a noisy room and the band tiles are jittering on HVAC or crowd murmur, set the noise-floor gate. With audio playing, press Shift+T to sample the current rolling RMS and pin it as the threshold. Audio hops below the threshold publish zeroed level and hit uniforms — the band tiles go silent under the floor.

The threshold also exposes through OSC at /audio/threshold (see OSC Routes) for show-control automation.

docs.title: 7. Where to go next
docs.text:
The rest of the help corpus expands on each surface:

  • Audio Reactivity — the full uniform catalog, the eight-to-four band reduction, and a worked radial-pulse shader example.
  • Scene Workflow — the .chroma package format, the load lifecycle, and the live-reload policy authors rely on while iterating.
  • Library Workflow — scene sources, the four-subdirectory bundled taxonomy, thumbnails, and the indexer.
  • Perform Mode — the five panels, the Snap bar, the scene rail, and the adapter-pill status surface.
  • Hotkey Reference — the canonical fifty-seven row hotkey vocabulary.
  • OSC Routes — wire-level routing and the network-conservative defaults.
  • Settings Reference — every setting in the Settings view, with the audio / graphics / storage / network / entitlement sections enumerated.

For an exhaustive verification checklist of every Wave 2.x acceptance gate plus the known synthetic surfaces, the release-eng pre-alpha smoke checklist (in the repository at release-eng/pre-alpha-smoke-checklist.md) is the source of truth. This quickstart is the operator-facing narrative; the smoke checklist is the test matrix.

docs.title: Scene Workflow
docs.text: A Chromaticity scene is an on-disk package that the runtime loads, compiles, and executes. This page covers the package layout, the load lifecycle, and the live-reload behaviour authors rely on while iterating.

docs.title: Scene package layout
docs.text:
The native package extension is .chroma. A package is a plain directory; the runtime accepts both the on-disk directory form and the .chromaPack zip transport form. The directory contains a small fixed set of files:

File Required Purpose scene.json yes Schema metadata, control declarations, pass declarations main.glsl yes Fragment-shader body for the single-pass entry point script.js no Optional script-host module: setup(), update(dt), transition() glsl/*.glsl no Shared GLSL include files images/* no Bundled media samplers used by the scene data/* reserved Reserved for the post-MVP external-data ingestion surface

The reference application's .synScene packages are accepted as import input only through the one-way Shadertoy / ISF / reference-show converters — they are never executed in place. See Library Workflow for how imported packages surface in the library after conversion.

docs.title: The load lifecycle
docs.text:
When a scene loads, it transitions through a fixed lifecycle: Unloaded → Loaded → Ready → Running. The Paused, Error, and Stopped terminal states are reachable from Running. Each transition is observable through the runtime's diagnostics console.

The compile pipeline runs in this order:

  1. Parse and validate scene.json against the canonical schema.
  2. Build the canonical internal scene model (controls, passes, transitions, media bindings, script lifecycle metadata).
  3. Preprocess GLSL — apply meta-pipeline includes and helpers.
  4. Compile shader stages and resolve the pass graph.
  5. Initialise the script sandbox, register lifecycle events.
  6. Bind resource descriptors (passes, images, media slots).

The loader runs in two modes. Strict mode enforces the canonical schema and hard-fails on contract violations; this is the default for new authoring. Compatibility mode accepts legacy keys and observed outliers from the compat-syn-v1 corpus, normalises them to the canonical model, and emits warnings — this is the mode the importers target.

docs.title: Controls and passes
docs.text:
Controls are typed parameters declared in scene.json under the CONTROLS array. Every control carries a NAME, TYPE, default, and optional range. The runtime exposes each control as a uniform of the matching GLSL type and as a script-host accessor; see the Hotkey Reference for the keyboard bindings that operate on the focused control.

Passes are declared under the PASSES array. Single-pass scenes leave PASSES empty and use main.glsl directly; multipass scenes name each pass and reference earlier passes via the multipass uniforms documented under Chromaticity Uniforms.

docs.title: Live reload while authoring
docs.text:
The authoring environment watches every file in the active package and applies a per-file reload policy:

!!! note "Live-reload policy by file type"

- `scene.json` — full scene rebuild; control state preserved where
  `NAME` is unchanged across the edit.
- `main.glsl` — recompile only; control values, script state, and
  pass targets are preserved as long as pass declarations are
  unchanged.
- `glsl/*.glsl` — same as `main.glsl` for every scene currently
  using the include.
- `script.js` — rebind the script host, re-run `setup()`, keep
  control values, reset script-local state.
- `images/*` — reload the affected sampler; everything else is
  preserved.

The shader-edit-to-visible-result latency budget is p95 ≤ 500 ms on the MVP hardware class. Hot reloads are not allowed to drop output frames; if a recompile exceeds the frame budget, the new shader is swapped in on the next frame boundary.

docs.title: Transitions
docs.text: Each scene declares its accepted transition shapes through the HARD_TRANSITIONS and SMOOTH_TRANSITIONS keys. Transition triggers are tied to runtime transition events (manual cuts, audio-driven cues, playlist advancement). Transition variables are projected into scene uniforms before pass execution so authors can sample them in GLSL or JavaScript.

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text:
The authoring console streams diagnostics from every subsystem (GLSL compiler, JS host, OSC and MIDI adapters, audio adapter, media adapter) tagged with timestamp, subsystem, scene name, and severity. The coerce severity covers every compatibility-mode coercion the loader applies — useful when porting reference scenes to the canonical model.

GLSL compile errors map back to the author's source line through a post-prepend mapping table, so the meta-pipeline header injected at compile time does not skew line numbers. JSON schema violations link directly to the offending path.

docs.title: Settings Reference
docs.text: Settings is where operators bring up the audio device, configure the output pipeline, register storage paths, and review the entitlement surface. The view is laid out as four operator-bring-up sections at the top, followed by the General toggles, the Hotkeys reference, and the Theme switcher.

docs.title: 1. Audio Device
docs.text:
The Audio Device section enumerates host audio devices through the audio adapter's input and output pickers. The fields surfaced are:

  • Input device — the microphone or capture interface feeding the analysis pipeline.
  • Output device — the playback target the runtime mixes to.
  • Sample rate — typically 48 kHz on macOS, 44.1 kHz on Windows consumer hardware.
  • Latency hint — low, balanced, or high. Lower hints reduce the wallclock between an audio event and its visual response, at the cost of buffer-underrun risk under CPU pressure.
  • Channel layout — the input channel mapping used by the mono mix-down.
  • Input gain — pre-AGC trim in dB.
  • Live level / peak meter — confirms the chosen device is producing signal before scene launch.

Input device selection, DJ stereo-pair routing, and pre-AGC input gain hot-swap live without restarting Chromaticity or interrupting stage output (backed by AppState::hot_swap_audio_input and lock-free atomic gain/pair handles).

docs.title: 2. Graphics and Output
docs.text:
The Graphics section covers everything between the renderer and the display:

  • Resolution — preset list (1080p, 1440p, 4K, …) plus a custom width × height entry. The custom entry is gated by the render.custom-resolution capability.
  • Render scale — fractional under-sample for performance-budget bring-up; defaults to 1.0.
  • Target FPS — the render-loop ceiling. Lower targets free GPU headroom for heavy multipass scenes.
  • V-Sync — when enabled, the present pacing is tied to the display's refresh; when disabled, the renderer free-runs at the FPS target.
  • HDR target — capability-gated; reserved for V2 hardware that exposes a 10-bit HDR swap chain.
  • Display assignment — selects which physical display the output window paints to in multi-display setups.

!!! note "Preference persistence vs. live runtime enforcement"

All Graphics preferences above persist cleanly to `settings.toml`
across restarts. Live runtime enforcement for Resolution, Render
scale, Target FPS, V-Sync, and HDR swap-chain output remains
planned (see `52-parity-coverage-matrix.md`).

docs.title: 3. Storage
docs.text:
The Storage section pins the filesystem locations the runtime reads and writes:

  • Media folders — directories searched for IMAGE_PATH, video samplers, and the per-scene images/ symlink targets.
  • Custom scene folders — extra directories merged into the library results alongside <UserDataRoot>/Scenes/. See Library Workflow for how merging works.
  • Backups path — destination for crash-restore snapshots and show-bundle exports, with a configurable retention window.
  • Cache cleanup (planned) — reserved buttons to clear the thumbnail cache and the shader-compile cache once disk-backed caches ship (currently displayed as disabled in Settings).

Each path field has a Browse button that invokes the native folder-picker through the shell IPC layer.

docs.title: 4. Network and adapter defaults
docs.text:
Chromaticity ships network-conservative by default — every adapter binds to loopback unless the operator explicitly opts in. The defaults matter because OSC and NDI carry no built-in authentication:

Adapter Default bind Opt-in path OSC inbound 127.0.0.1 (loopback) Operator selects an interface or 0.0.0.0 OSC outbound 127.0.0.1 target Operator sets per-subscriber target IP NDI input local subnet discovery Operator restricts to allowlist NDI output local subnet advertise Operator sets local-host-only or denylist Syphon and Spout local-host only n/a (protocol constraint)

Per-mapping source-IP allowlists honour CIDR notation (192.168.1.0/24) so a venue-Wi-Fi setup can trust a single subnet without opening every interface. Inbound traffic is rate-limited at 1000 messages per second per adapter (hard cap) and 100 messages per second per (adapter, route) pair (operator-floor default).

!!! warning "Changing a network setting may expose Chromaticity to the network"

Every override on this surface carries the explicit warning above.
Overrides are persisted per show, so exporting a `.chromaShow`
bundle reproduces the operator's network posture on the
destination machine.

See OSC Routes for the route taxonomy and payload hardening defaults the OSC adapter enforces.

!!! note "Live transport status"

Network and live-source preferences persist cleanly to
`settings.toml`. OSC inbound/outbound transport is live; live
runtime enforcement for NDI and Syphon/Spout texture transport
remains planned (see `52-parity-coverage-matrix.md`).

docs.title: 5. Entitlement and capabilities
docs.text:
Settings surfaces the active entitlement token and the resolved capability bitmask. Chromaticity's entitlement model is data-only — the runtime evaluates per-capability flags against a single in-memory EntitlementSet; there is no runtime concept of an "edition".

The following capabilities ship unconditionally free in every install, including with no token present:

  • Pause and transport control.
  • Hard-cut transitions (transitions-off).
  • Playlist navigation (next, previous, select).
  • Preset recall and Snap slots.
  • Scene export (for backup or hand-off).
  • OSC and MIDI route discovery messages.
  • Camera input (io.camera).

Capabilities that gate behind a valid token include the watermark removal (render.watermark.off), the OSC and Syphon I/O surfaces, the in-app authoring environment (authoring.ide), Shadertoy and ISF import (authoring.import), scene editing (authoring.edit), and the custom-resolution surface (render.custom-resolution).

docs.title: 6. Theme
docs.text: The Theme switcher cycles among the three shipped themes (Pulse, Atelier, Console). Themes are aesthetic options — they swap colour palettes and surface treatments without changing layout or workflow.

docs.title: Supported Formats and Codecs
docs.text:
A reference for every format Chromaticity ingests and emits. The runtime is deliberately narrow at MVP: a small, well-tested set of audio sample formats, one native scene package shape (plus a one-way Shadertoy import), and a small image set used for thumbnails. Video input, recording, and signed show bundles are documented honestly with their current wiring status — some are wired, several are deferred to post-MVP follow-ups, and a few are reject-with-diagnostic by design.

The wiring status column uses three states:

  • Wired — implemented and exercised by tests; available on the default build.
  • Synthetic — surface implemented to its public contract, but the concrete backend is a stub or fixture pending a follow-up.
  • Deferred — intentionally out of scope at MVP; tracked for a future wave.

docs.title: Audio input
docs.text: Audio capture goes through our patched cpal crate (third_party/cpal-0.17.1-patched), including zero-install macOS Core Audio Process Tap system-audio loopback (capturing Rekordbox 7 PC MASTER OUT without BlackHole) and multi-channel DJ Master-vs-Cue stereo-pair extraction (DDJ-FLX10, DJM-A9). cpal opens the host default input device (or configured System Audio / DJ interface) at startup and supports zero-restart live device and gain hot-swap from Settings (see Settings Reference). The audio analysis thread mixes the selected stereo pair down to mono, runs RMS / peak / 8-band FFT / BPM, and publishes one AudioUniformSnapshot per analysis hop; see Audio Reactivity for the analysis pipeline.

docs.title: Sample formats
docs.text:
cpal can deliver many sample formats; Chromaticity converts everything to f32 in the cpal callback before the analyser sees the frame.

cpal SampleFormat Status Conversion to f32 Common host f32 Wired Passthrough macOS (CoreAudio), Windows (WASAPI) i16 Wired s / i16::MAX Linux (ALSA default on many devices) u16 Wired (s - 32768) / 32768 Windows (occasional WASAPI default) i8 / u8 Rejected AudioError::CpalDeviceCapture reason at stream build i32 / u32 Rejected AudioError::CpalDeviceCapture reason at stream build i64 / u64 / f64 Rejected AudioError::CpalDeviceCapture reason at stream build

Unsupported sample formats fail loudly at stream build with a human-readable reason; the runtime does not silently transcode formats outside the supported set.

The i16 and u16 conversions are exact divisions by integer constants. i16::MIN maps to -1.00003... (slightly below -1.0 from two's-complement asymmetry) — the analyser tolerates the minority case through its clamp.

docs.title: Channel count and sample rate
docs.text:
Chromaticity is host-format-tolerant on the input side:

Property Behaviour Channel count Accepts any device-reported channel count; mixed to mono in analysis Sample rate Accepts the device default config; canonical analysis baseline is 48 kHz, hop cadence 375 Hz Buffer size cpal default for the host; the analyser is non-blocking and tolerates back-pressure via the bounded channel between cpal and the analyser

If the host has no audio subsystem (CI, headless, a Linux box without ALSA), device enumeration collapses to an empty list and the analyser falls back to a silent source rather than erroring.

docs.title: Default-input behaviour by platform
docs.text:
The "default input device" is platform-dependent and can surprise operators on first run.

Platform Default input device macOS CoreAudio default input, plus zero-install System Audio (Process Tap) loopback (ADR-022) selectable in Settings → Audio without BlackHole. Windows OS-selected default recording device (WASAPI). Linux ALSA default; varies by host configuration.

On macOS, select System Audio in Settings → Audio to react directly to system output (including Rekordbox 7 PC MASTER OUT) with zero virtual drivers. Virtual loopbacks (BlackHole, Loopback, VB-Cable) also work if desired.

docs.title: Scene packages
docs.text:
Chromaticity has one native scene format and a one-way Shadertoy import. Other scene formats either round-trip-convert or are rejected with a diagnostic.

Format Status Direction Notes .chroma Wired Read + author Directory package; canonical native scene format. Mandatory scene.json at the root. .chromaPack Deferred Read Zip-transport wrapper around a .chroma directory. Reserved; not yet wired. Shadertoy URL Wired Read (one-way) Converter wraps the Shadertoy body in a .chroma shell. See Import Shadertoy. .synScene Wired Read (conversion) Non-destructive .synScene -> .chroma importer wired in Import (commands/import.rs). ISF (.fs) Reject Reject Imports surface a diagnostic; native ISF execution deferred to V2.

docs.title: .chroma package layout
docs.text:
A .chroma package is a directory whose name ends in .chroma. The loader rejects any other extension and any non-directory path. The required entry is scene.json at the package root.

my-scene.chroma/
├── scene.json        # required, JSON root
├── main.glsl         # optional, fragment shader
├── script.js         # optional, scene-author script
└── images/           # optional, scene-author asset bundle

The wire format for scene.json is documented under the in-app Scene Workflow and Chroma Uniforms pages; key root keys include SCHEMA_VERSION, TITLE, CREDIT, DESCRIPTION, TAGS, CATEGORIES, CONTROLS, and PASSES. Unknown root keys are preserved in an extensions map rather than rejected, so authoring tools can add new metadata without breaking loaders.

docs.title: What is NOT imported
docs.text:
The Shadertoy import path is intentionally narrow:

  • Multi-buffer Shadertoy compositions — out of scope for the V1 import; a multipass-import pathway is a future-wave ADR.
  • Sound shaders — Chromaticity is a visual runtime; Shadertoy sound-shader bodies are rejected.
  • VR mode (mainVR) — rejected; no plausible auto-mapping into a single-pass mainImage.
  • ISF (.fs) — reject-with-diagnostic at MVP per design.

See Import Shadertoy for the full converter behaviour.

docs.title: Images
docs.text:
Image support is narrow because Chromaticity is a procedural-visuals runtime, not an image-processing host. The current consumers are scene thumbnails, Library cover images, and (for imported Shadertoy scenes) iChannel texture binding slots.

Image format Status Used for Notes PNG Wired Scene thumbnails, Library cover images Operator-supplied PNGs are loaded through the standard asset path. JPEG Wired Library cover images, iChannel texture binding Standard .jpg / .jpeg. GIF Deferred — No animated-GIF playback at MVP. HEIC / WebP Deferred — Not in scope; convert externally. Cubemaps Deferred — Shadertoy mainCubemap entrypoint is deferred to a future multipass-import pathway.

Scene thumbnails are rendered live on the GPU via render_scene_thumbnail (Metal/wgpu) with an in-memory LRU cache, falling back to a deterministic placeholder only when a scene has no main.glsl.

docs.title: Video
docs.text:
Video input and output are partially scaffolded but not wired end-to-end at MVP.

Surface Status Notes Camera capture (input) Synthetic CameraAdapter trait + NokhwaInputAdapter surface ship; per-platform concrete bindings (input-avfoundation on macOS, input-msmf on Windows) are deferred. bind returns DeviceNotFound; enumerate returns an empty list until the deferred backend lands. Webcam in scenes Deferred Shadertoy iChannel webcam mapping is reserved with a diagnostic; the body still compiles, but no live webcam feed binds at MVP. Syphon input (macOS) Synthetic SyphonInputAdapter surface ships per ADR-021. Concrete cross-process consumption is gated behind the Wave 1c-β Send-trait reconciliation + directory observer follow-ups. Syphon output (macOS) Synthetic SyphonOutputAdapter surface ships; publish_syphon_output real-impl is a deferred follow-up. Spout (Windows) Deferred Not yet scoped; the Syphon adapter is macOS-only by design. Video file playback Wired (Mix) Local .mp4 / .webm / image layers and Direct YouTube URL stream-in play live inside the Mix deck (liveMediaStore); native GPU texture decode for GLSL chroma_Media samplers remains planned.

docs.title: Camera pixel formats (planned)
docs.text:
The camera adapter surface declares the following pixel-format taxonomy so the deferred backend wave can attach without breaking the public contract. Byte order is named explicitly in every variant to avoid the ambiguity that has historically broken multi-year regression cycles in upstream camera codecs.

Variant Layout Bgra32 Bytes B, G, R, A in memory; 4-byte stride. Rgb24 Bytes R, G, B in memory; no alpha; 3-byte stride. Nv12 Planar Y' (full-res luma) + interleaved U/V at 4:2:0 chroma subsampling. Yuyv Packed Y0, U, Y1, V repeating (4:2:2 chroma subsampling); stride width * 2. Mjpeg Complete JPEG bitstream (SOI...EOI). Decoded to Bgra32 / Rgb24 at the render-side wiring (deferred).

Syphon textures are pinned to BGRA8Unorm per ADR-021 — the format universally supported across Syphon consumers on macOS.

docs.title: Recording and export
docs.text: Surface Status Notes .chroma scene export Wired Saving a scene from the in-app authoring environment is a free-tier capability. .chromaShow show bundle Synthetic Format harness ships: tar container with a flat manifest.json plus per-file SHA-256 + manifest SHA-256. Recovery / rollback semantics are Phase-4+ scope; bundle-level ed25519 signing is EV-ENTITLEMENT-ENFORCEMENT scope and layers on top of the checksum surface. Output recording (video) Planned Crash-safe Fmp4Muxer + ReplayBuffer ship in engine/runtime; standalone hardware H.264/AAC packet encoding remains Phase 7a. Output recording (audio) Planned System audio capture (macOS Core Audio Process Tap) is wired for live analysis and Twitch RTMPS; standalone file recording muxing remains Phase 7a. Screenshot (PNG) Deferred Not yet wired through the rendering backend.

docs.title: .chromaShow container shape
docs.text:
The bundle is a tar archive — not a zip — chosen on determinism grounds: identical inputs in identical order produce byte-identical output. The container carries:

  • A flat manifest.json at the archive root listing every payload entry plus its SHA-256.
  • Each payload at the path declared in the manifest.
  • A self-elided manifest SHA-256 (computed over the canonical JSON of the manifest with the manifest_sha256 field elided) for tamper detection on the file list itself.

Path-traversal defence is structural: tar entries that are not in the manifest path-set fail at the entry-iteration boundary; paths with .. segments, absolute paths, and Windows drive prefixes are rejected before archive emission. Compression, if ever wanted, layers on top (.chromaShow.gz) as a transport-only concern that does not perturb the format-conformance corpus.

docs.title: What this page does NOT cover
docs.text:
• OSC / MIDI wire formats — Open Sound Control and MIDI are control protocols, not codecs. See OSC Routes and Settings → MIDI for those surfaces.
  • GLSL dialects — Shader-side format coverage (Shadertoy iChannel uniforms, native chroma_* symbols) is documented in Chroma Uniforms.
  • Render-output codecs — There is no rendered-output codec surface at MVP; the live preview targets the in-app window, not a file. Output capture is a deferred follow-up.

docs.title: System Requirements
docs.text: Concrete system-requirements reference for Chromaticity. The tables below describe the minimum, recommended, and known-limited configurations the runtime is engineered against. The figures are pragmatic operator guidance rather than certified hardware floors — deterministic performance on any specific rig depends on the active scene, the audio analysis load, and which adapters are enabled.

docs.title: 1. Supported platforms
docs.text:
Chromaticity ships as a Tauri 2 desktop binary built against the Rust 2024 edition (MSRV 1.85.0). Today's bundle targets are:

Platform Status Notes macOS 12 Monterey+ (Apple Silicon) Supported Primary development target. Metal backend via wgpu. macOS 12 Monterey+ (Intel x86_64) Pending Wave 2.10 Lane A Build target exists; bundle + signing pipeline rides the Lane A widening. Windows 10 (1809+) / Windows 11 (x86_64) Supported DX12 primary, Vulkan fallback. Linux (x86_64, glibc ≥ 2.31) Pending Wave 2.10 Lane A Vulkan backend. Bundle pipeline + AppImage / .deb targets land with Lane A. 32-bit x86 / ARMv7 / iOS / Android Not supported No work planned.

The Mac Intel and Linux entries above reflect the active widening pending in Wave 2.10 Lane A — the engine and shell already compile against both targets, but the signing / bundle / appcast pipeline remains macOS-arm64 + Windows-x86_64 only at the Wave 1e-γ scaffold.

docs.title: 2. CPU and RAM floors
docs.text:
Audio analysis runs on a dedicated cpal capture thread and the FFT / BPM pipeline is single-threaded; scene rendering runs on a wgpu device thread. The CPU floor reflects the latter — comfortable headroom for audio analysis is well below the floors below.

Tier CPU RAM Notes Minimum 4-core x86_64 / Apple Silicon, ≥ 2.0 GHz 8 GB Single-output workflow, lighter scenes, no multipass post-stack. Recommended 6-core+ at ≥ 3.0 GHz; Apple M1 / M2 / M3 / M4 16 GB Headroom for shader compile, library thumbnailing, OSC + MIDI together. Comfortable 8-core+; Apple M-series Pro / Max; Ryzen 7 / i7 / i9 32 GB Heavy multipass scenes, ≥ 1440p output, parallel scene authoring.

The runtime forbids unsafe Rust workspace-wide and the release profile builds with lto = "fat" and a single codegen unit; binaries land in the small-low-hundreds-of-MB range and idle RAM use is typically 200-400 MB before any scene is loaded.

docs.title: 3. GPU floors and adapter selection
docs.text:
Chromaticity selects a GPU adapter deterministically at launch per ADR-011 §7. The selection helper (engine/render::adapter_selection) ranks every enumerated adapter on the lexicographic tuple:

  1. operator override (if a persisted adapter ID still matches);
  2. adapter-type rank (Discrete > Integrated > Virtual > CPU > Other);
  3. backend-rank (Metal on macOS, DX12 on Windows, Vulkan on Linux);
  4. battery-friendly flag (flips Integrated above Discrete when set);
  5. alphabetic name tie-break for full determinism.
Tier GPU VRAM Notes Minimum Integrated GPU with wgpu-supported backend shared Apple M-series, Intel Iris Xe, AMD Radeon iGPU, modern Linux integrated GPUs. Recommended Discrete GPU released 2020 or later ≥ 4 GB NVIDIA RTX 30/40 series, AMD RX 6000/7000 series, Apple M-Pro/M-Max. Comfortable Workstation discrete GPU ≥ 8 GB Headroom for 4K output, heavy multipass, future HDR target work.

docs.title: Dual-GPU laptops
docs.text:
On laptops with both an integrated and a discrete GPU the default posture is to pin the discrete adapter for performance. The persisted operator override (Settings → Output → GPU dropdown) is honoured ahead of the type-rank — set it when you want to pin a specific adapter across launches. If the persisted adapter is no longer attached (an unplugged eGPU, for example) the selector silently falls through to the next-best adapter rather than refusing to launch.

A future widening will surface a power-source-aware battery preference + a TDR-history warning when the selected Windows adapter has reported device-removed events in the last 24 hours; the policy plumbing is in place, the UI banner is not yet wired.

docs.title: 4. Audio interface guidance
docs.text:
Audio capture binds the host's default input device by default on each platform. On macOS that resolves to the built-in microphone (not system audio output); routing system audio through Chromaticity requires a virtual loopback driver (BlackHole, Loopback, or equivalent) configured as the default input. On Windows the equivalent is WASAPI loopback or Voicemeeter; on Linux, a PulseAudio / PipeWire monitor source.

Property Floor Recommended Interface Built-in input Class-compliant USB or Thunderbolt Sample rate 44.1 kHz 48 kHz Bit depth 16-bit 24-bit Channel count Mono (analysis is mono-mix) Stereo Buffer / latency hint balanced low on capable hardware

The analysis pipeline mixes input down to mono before FFT / RMS / peak extraction so multichannel interfaces are not necessary for visual reactivity. The latency_hint field on the Audio settings (low / balanced / high) trades audio-to-visual response latency against buffer-underrun resilience under CPU pressure. Audio devices do not hot-swap mid-show — changes apply at the next analysis-thread restart (typically the next scene load).

docs.title: 5. MIDI device guidance
docs.text:
MIDI is provided by midir 0.10 and the platform's native MIDI stack: CoreMIDI on macOS, WinMM on Windows, ALSA seq on Linux. Any class-compliant USB MIDI controller works without a vendor driver.

Surface Supported Notes USB MIDI controllers Class-compliant, no vendor driver Pads, knobs, faders, transport surfaces. 5-pin DIN MIDI Through a class-compliant USB adapter Standard DIN-to-USB interfaces. Bluetooth MIDI Apple BLE-MIDI on macOS Subject to OS pairing latency. Network MIDI (RTP) Through OS-side virtual port Configured outside Chromaticity.

What the adapter parses and surfaces today: Note On / Off, Control Change (7-bit), Pitch Bend, Program Change, Channel Pressure, Polyphonic Aftertouch, and 14-bit CC pairs. MPE is intentionally deferred to V2 with a diagnostic-fires-once rejection. SysEx is logged-only.

MIDI learn captures a single message at a time at this build; the binding-to-control wire is a known follow-up.

docs.title: 6. Network
docs.text:
Chromaticity binds every network adapter to loopback (127.0.0.1) by default per ADR-013. Exposing OSC or any other inbound adapter on a routable interface is an explicit operator opt-in in the Settings view, and overrides carry an explicit "may expose Chromaticity to the network" warning.

Property Default Configurable in Settings OSC inbound bind 127.0.0.1 Yes OSC inbound port 9000 / UDP Yes OSC outbound target 127.0.0.1 Yes (per subscriber) OSC outbound port 9001 / UDP Yes Maximum OSC packet size 64 KiB No (hard cap) Maximum OSC bundle depth 4 No (hard cap) Per-route rate limit 100 msgs/sec Yes (floor 100) Per-adapter rate cap 1000 msgs/sec No (hard cap) NDI / Syphon / Spout Local subnet / host Local-only by protocol

No outbound network traffic occurs at startup without an explicit operator action. Crash payloads are redacted before write, settings files persist locally, and the updater endpoint (when configured) talks only to the staging or production appcast URL pinned in the Tauri config.

docs.title: 7. Storage
docs.text:
Persistent operator state lives in the platform-native per-user app data directory through Tauri's app.path().app_data_dir() resolver:

Platform Directory macOS ~/Library/Application Support/app.chromaticity.desktop/ Windows %APPDATA%\app.chromaticity.desktop\ Linux $XDG_DATA_HOME/app.chromaticity.desktop/ (typically ~/.local/share/app.chromaticity.desktop/)

Files written into that directory today:

File Purpose settings.toml Persisted Audio / Graphics / Storage / General settings, theme, OSC ports. settings.toml.malformed-<timestamp> Quarantined copy of an unparseable settings file. Hand-correctable. crash-resume.bin Crash-resume snapshot for next-launch state restoration.

Settings persistence uses TOML so operators can hand-correct a file the runtime cannot parse; a malformed file is quarantined before the next save so the damaged file is preserved for repair. New settings fields land with serde(default) so an older settings.toml continues to deserialise cleanly under a newer build.

Disk-space footprint at install is typically under 200 MB. The thumbnail cache and the shader-compile cache live under the same app data directory and can be cleared from Settings → Storage.

docs.title: 8. Display, input, and ergonomic guidance
docs.text:
Property Floor Recommended Display size 1440 × 900 1920 × 1080+ for Perform; 2560 × 1440+ for Author. Output displays Single output Dedicated output display for visuals, separate operator display for chrome. Pointer input Mouse or trackpad Trackpad gestures for parameter scrubbing; tablet stylus for swatch / curve work. Keyboard Standard layout The 57-row hotkey catalogue assumes a standard layout; remappers work but are not validated.

The application window opens at 1280 × 800 by default and is resizable. Perform-class views are designed to fit ~1440 × 900 without page-level scrolling; specific inner panels (long scene lists, the hotkey catalogue) scroll within their container.

docs.text:
